note: Church history for the timeline, from the apostles to the present. Every date is its source's own, and every event quotes the source's words for it (source.quote; a life quotes birth and death, the second in second_source where one passage does not give both). Sources, in order of preference: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church (8 vols.); Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom (3 vols.); the Ante-Nicene Fathers and Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers; The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge (1908-14). Quotes are copied from the plain text of the EPUBs in the app's library (file: the extracted .txt), except New Schaff-Herzog vols. III-VIII and X-XII, which CCEL holds only as page images: those quotes were transcribed from the CCEL page image named in file. Web sources are used only where these works do not reach, for the six events after 1914; each such event has two independent references that agree on the date (source and second_source). Dates are not corrected: they are Julian (Old Style) where the source reckons so, and circa marks a date the source gives as approximate or disputed. Era bounds are the app's arrangement; the first six follow the periods of Schaff's History. What is kept: councils, creeds and confessions; the Reformers, the Puritans and the theologians the app's library reads; persecutions and turning points of the whole church; the founding moments of Protestant missions; and milestones in the history of the Bible's text and translation. Popular modern evangelists, ecumenical and parachurch bodies, and the internal milestones of other movements are left out. Each event's id is permanent, because the app names an event by it: a new event takes the next unused number wherever it falls in the file, and no id is renumbered or reused. See SOURCES.md.

events.title: Claudius expels the Jews from Rome
events.note: The earliest trace of Christianity in Rome: Suetonius records that Claudius banished the Jews over commotions stirred up by "Chrestus", probably disputes between Jews and Christians. Aquila and Priscilla were among those expelled (Acts 18:2).

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The first historic trace of Christianity in Rome we have in a notice of the heathen historian Suetonius, confirmed by Luke, that Claudius, about a.d. 52, banished the Jews from Rome

events.title: Martyrdom of James, the Lord's brother
events.note: James the Just, head of the church at Jerusalem, was stoned at the instigation of the high priest Ananus, according to Josephus. Hegesippus places his death a few years later, shortly before the siege of Jerusalem.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 27. James the Brother of the Lord.
source.quote: stoned to death with some others, as "breakers of the law," i.e. Christians, in the interval between the procuratorship of Festus and that of Albinus, that is, in the year 63.

events.title: Great fire of Rome and Nero's persecution
events.note: Fire broke out in Rome on the night of 18-19 July 64 and burned for more than a week. Nero cast the blame on the Christians, and a "vast multitude" of them were put to death in the first imperial persecution.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 37. The Roman Conflagration and the Neronian Persecution.
source.quote: The first of these imperial persecutions with which the Martyrdom of Peter and Paul is connected by ecclesiastical tradition, took place in the tenth year of Nero’s reign, a.d. 64

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.locator: § 37. The Roman Conflagration and the Neronian Persecution.
second_source.quote: It broke out in the night between the 18th and 19th of July, among the wooden shops in the south-eastern end of the Great Circus, near the Palatine hill.

events.title: Martyrdom of Paul in Rome
events.note: Paul was put to death under Nero; as a Roman citizen he was beheaded rather than crucified, by tradition near the Ostian Way outside Rome. The year is disputed, with views ranging from 64 to 69.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The public life of Paul, from the third year after his conversion to his martyrdom, a.d. 40–64, embraces a quarter of a century

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: As to the year of his death, the views vary from a.d. 64 to 69.

events.title: Martyrdom of Peter in Rome
events.note: The uniform tradition of the early church holds that Peter preached in Rome and was crucified there in Nero's persecution. The year cannot be fixed: it fell after July 64 and is variously given as any year from 64 to 69.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 25. The Church of Jerusalem and the Labors of Peter.
source.quote: Nor can we fix the year of his martyrdom, except that it must have taken place after July, 64, when the Neronian persecution broke out (according to Tacitus). It is variously assigned to every year between 64 and 69.

events.title: The Jewish War against Rome
events.note: Judaea rose in revolt in May 66 under the procurator Gessius Florus; Vespasian and then his son Titus led the Roman campaign, which ended with the siege and fall of Jerusalem in 70. The Christians of Jerusalem left the city and took refuge at Pella beyond the Jordan.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 38. The Jewish War and the Destruction of Jerusalem. a.d. 70.
source.quote: At last, in the month of May, a.d. 66, under the last procurator, Gessius Florus (from 65 onward), a wicked and cruel tyrant who, as Josephus says, was placed as a hangman over evil-doers, an organized rebellion broke out against the Romans

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.locator: § 38. The Jewish War and the Destruction of Jerusalem. a.d. 70.
second_source.quote: In April, a.d. 70, immediately after the Passover, when Jerusalem was filled with strangers, the siege began.

events.title: John on Patmos writes the Revelation
events.note: John was banished to the island of Patmos, where he received the visions of the Revelation. The date is disputed: Schaff judged 68 or 69, under Nero, most probable, while the tradition beginning with Irenaeus places the exile under Domitian, about 95.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: We hold, then, as the most probable view, that John was exiled to Patmos under Nero, wrote the Apocalypse soon after Nero’s death, a.d. 68 or 69, returned to Ephesus

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: External evidence points to the reign of Domitian, a.d. 95; internal evidence to the reign of Nero, or soon after his death, a.d. 68.

events.title: Titus destroys Jerusalem and the temple
events.note: After a siege begun in April 70, Roman forces under Titus burned the temple on 10 August and razed the city. Only three towers of Herod's palace and part of the western wall were left standing.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 38. The Jewish War and the Destruction of Jerusalem. a.d. 70.
source.quote: It was burned on the tenth of August, a.d. 70, the same day of the year on which, according to tradition, the first temple was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar.

events.title: Josephus writes The Jewish War
events.note: Flavius Josephus, who went through the war first as a Jewish commander in Galilee and then as a companion of Titus, wrote its history as an eyewitness. It is the principal account of the siege and destruction of Jerusalem.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 38. The Jewish War and the Destruction of Jerusalem. a.d. 70.
source.quote: The history of the Jewish war was written by him as eye-witness about a.d. 75.

events.title: The Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles)
events.note: An anonymous church manual of Jewish-Christian origin: moral teaching in the form of the two ways, directions for baptism and the Lord's Supper, and rules for church offices. Lost for centuries, it was published by Bryennios in 1883.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The first Gospel was well known to the author of the "Didache of the Apostles," who wrote between 80 and 100, and made large use of it

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.locator: § 56. Collections of Ecclesiastical Law. The Apostolical Constitutions and Canons.
second_source.quote: The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles is the oldest and simplest church manual, of Jewish Christian (Palestinian or Syrian) origin, from the end of the first century, known to the Greek fathers, but only recently discovered and published by Bryennios (1883).

events.title: Domitian's persecution
events.note: Domitian treated the profession of Christianity as a crime against the state; his cousin the consul Flavius Clemens was put to death for "atheism" and Clemens's wife Domitilla was banished. His successor Nerva (96-98) recalled the exiles.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: A generation later two cousins of the Emperor Domitian (81–96), T. Flavius Clemens, consul (in 95), and his wife, Flavia Domitilla, were accused of "atheism, " that is, of Christianity, and condemned, the husband to death, the wife to exile (a.d. 96).

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: The Consul Flavius Clemens, Domitian’s cousin, who was put to death by him for "atheism" i.e. the Christian faith, a.d. 95, while his wife Domitilla (who founded the oldest Christian cemetery in Rome) was banished to an island.

events.title: Clement of Rome writes to the Corinthians
events.note: A letter sent in the name of the church at Rome to the divided church at Corinth, universally ascribed to Clement, calling it back to humility, peace and order. It is the first writing to mention the martyrdom of Peter.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 26. The Peter of History and the Peter of Fiction.
source.quote: Clement, bishop of Rome, who first, about a.d. 95, makes mention of Peter’s martyrdom

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: The oldest post-apostolic witness is Clement of Rome, who wrote about 95

events.title: Death of the apostle John at Ephesus
events.note: John, the last survivor of the apostles, spent his later years at Ephesus at the head of the churches of Asia Minor. He died there in extreme old age, in the reign of Trajan.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: He died there in extreme old age during the reign of Trajan, which began in 98.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: 10. The death of John after the accession of Trajan, a.d. 98 (according to general ecclesiastical tradition).

events.title: Martyrdom of Ignatius of Antioch
events.note: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, was condemned under Trajan and taken to Rome to be thrown to the beasts, writing letters to the churches on the way. Schaff gives the traditional year 107 but adds that it was probably between 110 and 116.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 17. Trajan. a.d. 98–117—Christianity Forbidden—Martyrdom of Symeon of Jerusalem, and Ignatius of Antioch.
source.quote: The emperor Trajan, in 107, came to Antioch, and there threatened with persecution all who refused to sacrifice to the gods. Ignatius was tried for this offence

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.locator: § 17. Trajan. a.d. 98–117—Christianity Forbidden—Martyrdom of Symeon of Jerusalem, and Ignatius of Antioch.
second_source.quote: In the same year (or probably between 110 and 116) the distinguished bishop Ignatius of Antioch was condemned to death, transported to Rome, and thrown before wild beasts in the Colosseum.

events.title: Bar Kokhba revolt
events.note: A second Jewish rising against Rome under the messianic pretender Bar-Cochba, who had Christians who would not join him put to death. After its defeat Jerusalem was rebuilt as the Roman colony Aelia Capitolina.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: the Jews were provoked to a new and powerful insurrection (a.d. 132–135). A pseudo-Messiah, Bar-Cochba (son of the stars, Num. 24:17), afterwards called Bar-Cosiba (son of falsehood), put himself at the head of the rebels

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.quote: BAR KOK´BA: The name traditionally assigned to the leader of the great insurrection of the Jews in Palestine against the Romans under the emperor Hadrian in the years 132-135

events.title: Marcion teaches at Rome
events.note: Marcion of Sinope rejected the Old Testament and its God, and made a canon of his own from an abridged Gospel of Luke and ten epistles of Paul. Polycarp, meeting him at Rome, called him "the first-born of Satan."

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: He betook himself, about the middle of the second century, to Rome (140–155), which originated none of the Gnostic systems, but attracted them all.

events.title: Justin Martyr's First Apology
events.note: Justin's defense of the Christians, addressed to the emperor Antoninus Pius, gives the first reliable account of the church's public worship and of baptism and the Lord's Supper.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The First or larger Apology (68 chapters) is addressed to the Emperor Antoninus Pius (137–161) and his adopted sons, and was probably written about a.d. 147, if not earlier

events.resource: ANF 01 The Apostolic Fathers with Justin Martyr and Irenaeus.epub

events.title: Tatian's Diatessaron
events.note: Tatian, a pupil of Justin Martyr, wove the four Gospels into one continuous narrative, the Diatessaron ("through the four").

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: But his extant apologetic treatise against the Gentiles, and his Gospel-Harmony (recently recovered), which were written between 153 and 170, show no clear traces of Gnosticism

events.resource: ANF 09 The Gospel of Peter, The Diatessaron of Tatian, The Apocalypse of Peter.epub

events.title: Martyrdom of Polycarp
events.note: Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna and a disciple of the apostle John, was burned at the stake after telling the proconsul he had served Christ eighty-six years. The Smyrnaean church's letter on his death is the oldest of the martyr-acts.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 19 Antoninus Pius. a.d. 137–161. The Martyrdom of Polycarp.
source.quote: The persecution of the church at Smyrna and the martyrdom of its venerable bishop, which was formerly assigned to the year 167, under the reign of Marcus Aurelius, took place, according to more recent research, under Antoninus in 155

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.quote: POLYCARP: Bishop of Smyrna and martyr; b. in the second half of the first century; d. at Smyrna Feb. 23, 155.

events.title: Martyrdom of Justin Martyr
events.note: Justin, the foremost apologist of the second century, was scourged and beheaded at Rome with six other Christians after refusing to sacrifice before the city prefect Rusticus.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Here, at the instigation of a Cynic philosopher, Crescens, whom he had convicted of ignorance about Christianity, Justin, with six other Christians, about the year 166, was scourged and beheaded.

events.title: Muratorian Fragment on the canon
events.note: An early Roman list of New Testament books, named for Muratori, who discovered and first published it in 1740. Schaff elsewhere dates it between 170 and 180.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: But this fragment is of earlier date (a.d. 170), and written in Latin, though perhaps originally in Greek. It is as far as we know the oldest Latin church document of Rome, and of very great importance for the history of the canon.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.locator: § 138. The Holy Scriptures and the Canon. (note)
second_source.quote: is a fragment of Roman origin, though translated from the Greek, between a.d. 170 and 180

events.title: Irenaeus writes Against Heresies
events.note: Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons and a pupil of Polycarp, refuted the Gnostic systems in five books, appealing to the Scriptures and to the faith handed down in the apostolic churches.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: It was composed during the pontificate of Eleutherus, that is between the years 177 and 190.

events.resource: ANF 01 The Apostolic Fathers with Justin Martyr and Irenaeus.epub

events.title: Martyrs of Lyons and Vienne
events.note: Among the dead were the ninety-year-old bishop Pothinus and the slave girl Blandina. The churches' letter describing the persecution is preserved by Eusebius.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: In 177, the churches of Lyons and Vienne, in the South of France, underwent a severe trial.

events.title: Origen
events.note: The greatest scholar of his age: head of the catechetical school at Alexandria, later a teacher at Caesarea, compiler of the Hexapla and author of the first attempt at a complete system of Christian doctrine. Tortured in the Decian persecution, he died at Tyre in 253 or 254.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: He was born of Christian parents at Alexandria, in the year 185

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: he died some time after, at the age of sixty-nine, in the year 253 or 254, at Tyre

events.title: Clement heads the school of Alexandria
events.note: Clement of Alexandria, raised a heathen and converted in adult life after studying the schools of Greek philosophy, taught at the city's catechetical school, where Origen was among his pupils, until persecution drove him away.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: about A.D. 189 succeeded Pantaenus as president of the catechetical school of that city. Here he labored benignly some twelve years for the conversion of heathens and the education of the Christians, until, as it appears, the persecution under Septimius Severus in 202 compelled him to flee.

events.title: Easter controversy under Victor of Rome
events.note: Victor, bishop of Rome, demanded that the churches of Asia stop keeping the Christian Passover on the fourteenth of Nisan and threatened to excommunicate them. Polycrates of Ephesus protested, and Irenaeus rebuked Victor and pleaded for peace.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Much more important and vehement was the third stage of the controversy between 190 and 194, which extended over the whole church, and occasioned many synods and synodical letters

events.title: Pantaenus travels to India
events.note: Pantaenus, the Alexandrian teacher under whom Clement studied, is reported to have carried the gospel to India; Schaff finds this more credible than the legends of Thomas and Bartholomew.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: But a more credible statement is, that the Christian teacher Pantaeus of Alexandria journeyed to that country about 190, and that in the fourth century churches were found there.

events.title: Tertullian's Apology
events.note: Tertullian of Carthage, the father of Latin theology, answered pagan slanders against the Christians; the Apologeticus records the heathen remark, "Behold how they love one another!"

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: It was composed in the reign of Septimius Severus, between 197 and 200. It is unquestionably one of the most beautiful monuments of the heroic age of the church.

events.resource: ANF 03 Latin Christianity Its Founder, Tertullian.epub

events.title: Cyprian of Carthage
events.note: A wealthy rhetorician converted in mature age, Cyprian became bishop of Carthage about two years after his baptism, led his church through the Decian persecution and was beheaded under Valerian.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: sprang from a noble and wealthy heathen family of Carthage, where he was born about the year 200, or earlier.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: five sermons of Augustin still remain in memory of Cyprian’s martyrdom, Sept. 14, 258.

events.title: Tertullian embraces Montanism
events.note: Montanism, a prophetic and rigorist movement begun in Phrygia by Montanus about the middle of the second century, won its ablest defender in Tertullian, who stayed zealous for the catholic faith against the heretics.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: He became in the year 201 or 202, from ascetic sympathies, a most energetic and influential advocate of Montanism

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: Some years after, between 199 and 203, he joined the puritanic, though orthodox, sect of the Montanists.

events.title: Septimius Severus forbids conversion
events.note: The emperor's law against the further spread of Christianity and Judaism set off violent persecution in Egypt and North Africa; at Alexandria Leonides, the father of Origen, was beheaded.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 21. Condition of the Church from Septimius Severus to Philip the Arabian. a.d. 193–249.
source.quote: In the beginning of the third century (202) Septimius Severus, turned perhaps by Montanistic excesses, enacted a rigid law against the further spread both of Christianity and of Judaism.

events.title: Martyrdom of Perpetua and Felicitas
events.note: Perpetua, a young noblewoman with a nursing infant, and Felicitas, a slave, were thrown to wild beasts at Carthage. The account of their imprisonment preserves words from the martyrs' own prison diaries.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Two of the most distinguished female martyrs, Perpetua and Felicitas, were addicted to them, and died a heroic death at Carthage in the persecution of Septimius Severus (203).

events.title: Mani, founder of Manichaeism
events.note: A Persian teacher who blended Zoroastrian dualism with Christian elements and called himself the promised Paraclete. His sect spread across the Roman world; Augustine was a Manichaean for several years.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: of the third century (215–277), who came over to Christianity, or rather introduced some Christian elements into the Zoroastrian religion

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: was crucified, or flayed alive by order of king Behram I. (Veranes) about 277

events.title: Hippolytus banished to Sardinia
events.note: Hippolytus, the learned Roman presbyter who wrote the Refutation of All Heresies and opposed the bishops Zephyrinus and Callistus, was banished to the mines with bishop Pontianus and is thought to have died there.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: states that a "presbyter" Hippolytus was banished, together with the Roman bishop Pontianus, about 235, to the unhealthy island of Sardinia

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: He died a martyr in 235 or 236.

events.title: Gregory Thaumaturgus bishop in Pontus
events.note: A convert and pupil of Origen, Gregory "the Wonder-worker" is said to have found only seventeen Christians in his diocese and to have left only as many unbelievers at his death.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: labored as bishop of Neo-Caesarea in Pontus from 244 to 270 with extraordinary success.

events.title: Origen's Against Celsus
events.note: Origen's eight books answering the pagan philosopher Celsus's attack on Christianity, written in the last years of his life and preserved complete in the original.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The refutation of Celsus’s attack upon Christianity, in eight books, written in the last years of his life, about 248, is preserved complete in the original

events.resource: ANF 04 Fathers of the Third Century Tertullian, Part Fourth; Minucius Felix; Commodian.epub

events.title: Persecution under Decius
events.note: The first persecution to cover the whole empire. Many Christians sacrificed or bought false certificates, and the question of restoring these lapsed divided the church.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 22. Persecutions under Decius, and Valerian. a.d. 249–260. Martyrdom of Cyprian.
source.quote: Decius Trajan (249–251), an earnest and energetic emperor, in whom the old Roman spirit once more awoke, resolved to root out the church as an atheistic and seditious sect, and in the year 250 published an edict to all the governors of the provinces

events.title: Anthony of Egypt
events.note: Egyptian hermit regarded as the father of Christian monasticism; his Life was written by Athanasius. He died at about a hundred and five years of age.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 35. Paul of Thebes and St. Anthony.
source.quote: Anthony sprang from a Christian and honorable Coptic family, and was born about 251

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.locator: § 35. Paul of Thebes and St. Anthony.
second_source.quote: expired with a smiling face, in the year 356, a hundred and five years old

events.title: Cyprian's On the Unity of the Church
events.note: Written amid the schisms at Carthage and Rome, it teaches that there is one church, held together by its bishops, outside which there is no salvation: "No one can have God for his father, who has not the church for his mother."

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Among these is his tract on the Unity of the Church (A. D. 251), that "magna charta" of the old catholic high-church spirit

events.resource: ANF 05 Fathers of the Third Century Hippolytus, Cyprian, Caius, Novatian, Appendix.epub

events.title: Novatian schism
events.note: The Roman presbyter Novatian, opposing the readmission of the lapsed, was set up as a rival bishop to Cornelius. His strict party spread in East and West and lasted into the sixth century.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: forerunner of Novatianus, who was ordained anti pope in 251

events.title: Councils of Carthage on heretical baptism
events.note: Under Cyprian the African bishops ruled that converts baptized by heretics must be baptized in the church; Stephen of Rome held such baptism valid and broke off communion with them.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: He was followed by the North African church, which, in several councils at Carthage in the years 255–6, rejected heretical baptism

events.title: Persecution under Valerian
events.note: Clergy and prominent laymen were banished, their property confiscated and assemblies forbidden, and then the death penalty returned. Sixtus II of Rome and Cyprian of Carthage were among the martyrs.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 22. Persecutions under Decius, and Valerian. a.d. 249–260. Martyrdom of Cyprian.
source.quote: Valerian (253–260) was at first mild towards the Christians; but in 257 he changed his course, and made an effort to check the progress of their religion without bloodshed, by the banishment of ministers and prominent laymen

events.title: Gallienus grants the church peace
events.note: Gallienus ended the persecution and recognized Christianity as a lawful religion, opening some forty years of peace in which the church grew rapidly and built larger houses of worship.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Gallienus (260–268) gave peace to the church once more, and even acknowledged Christianity as a religio licita. And this calm continued forty years

events.title: Synods of Antioch against Paul of Samosata
events.note: Paul, bishop of Antioch, denied the personality of the Logos and taught that Christ rose to divine dignity by his own moral development. The third synod, in 269 or 268, deposed him.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 55. The Councils of Elvira, Arles, and Ancyra.
source.quote: three were held against Paul of Samosata in Antioch (264–269)

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.locator: § 150. Antitrinitarians. First Class: The Alogi, Theodotus, Artemon, Paul of Samosata.
second_source.quote: at a third synod held in Antioch a.d. 269 or 268, they pronounced his deposition.

events.title: Constantine the Great
events.note: The first Christian emperor, who ended the persecutions and called the Council of Nicaea. He was baptized on his deathbed in 337.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: was born probably in the year 272

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: and died a few days after, on Pentecost, May 22, 337

events.title: Athanasius of Alexandria
events.note: Bishop of Alexandria from 328 and the leading defender of the Nicene faith against Arianism, for which he was exiled five times. His birth is dated between 296 and 298.

source.work: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series
source.locator: Prolegomena, Chapter II. Life of St. Athanasius and Account of Arianism, §1. Early years, 298–319.
source.quote: Athanasius was born between 296 and 298.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: In the year 373 he died, after an administration of nearly forty-six years

events.title: The Great Persecution under Diocletian
events.note: The last and most violent persecution: churches were destroyed, the Scriptures burned, Christians stripped of civil rights and at last ordered to sacrifice on pain of death.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The persecution began on the twenty-third day of February, 303, the feast of the Terminalia (as if to make an end of the Christian sect), with the destruction of the magnificent church in Nicomedia

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: Galerius, the real author of the persecution, brought to reflection by a terrible disease, put an end to the slaughter shortly before his death, by a remarkable edict of toleration, which he issued from Nicomedia in 311

events.title: Council of Elvira
events.note: Nineteen bishops, mostly from southern Spain, passed eighty-one canons on church discipline and morals; the thirty-sixth forbade pictures on the walls of churches.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 55. The Councils of Elvira, Arles, and Ancyra.
source.quote: The Synod of Elvira (Illiberis, or Eliberis, probably on the site of the modern Granada) was held in 306

events.title: Galerius's edict of toleration
events.note: The dying Galerius allowed Christians to hold their assemblies again and asked them to pray for the emperors. Schaff reckons that it virtually closed the age of persecution, though Maximin kept up the oppression in the East for a time.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Galerius, the real author of the persecution, brought to reflection by a terrible disease, put an end to the slaughter shortly before his death, by a remarkable edict of toleration, which he issued from Nicomedia in 311, in connexion with Constantine and Licinius.

events.title: Constantine defeats Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge
events.note: Constantine defeated his rival Maxentius outside Rome and became master of the West. Eusebius and Lactantius connect the victory with Constantine's turn to the sign of the cross.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: defeated Maxentius in three battles; the last in October, 312, at the Milvian bridge, near Rome, where Maxentius found a disgraceful death in the waters of the Tiber.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: After this victory at Rome (which occurred October 27, 312)

events.title: Edict of Milan grants religious toleration
events.note: Constantine and his eastern colleague Licinius issued from Milan an edict granting full freedom of worship to all religions, with special reference to Christianity.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Constantine, in conjunction with his eastern colleague, Licinius, published in January, 313, from Milan, an edict of religious toleration

events.title: Athanasius writes On the Incarnation
events.note: The young Athanasius wrote the two-part work Against the Heathen and On the Incarnation of the Word, setting out why the Word of God became man. The editor dates it in or shortly before 318.

source.work: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series
source.locator: Against the Heathen (Contra Gentes): Introduction to the Treatise
source.quote: Hence the date usually adopted, viz. in or shortly before 318 A.D.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: Among these are the two able and enthusiastic kindred productions of his youth (composed before 325): “A Discourse against the Greeks,” and “On the Incarnation of the Divine Word,)

events.resource: NPNF2 04 Athanasius Select Works and Letters.epub

events.title: Constantine's Sunday law
events.note: Constantine forbade the sitting of courts and manual labor in the towns on Sunday, while leaving farm work free; Schaff counts him the founder of the civil observance of the day.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Constantine in 321 forbade the sitting of courts and all secular labor in towns on “the venerable day of the sun,” as he expresses himself

events.title: Eusebius completes his Church History
events.note: Eusebius of Caesarea finished the ten books of his Church History, the first full history of the church from the apostles to his own day, which earned him the name father of church history.

source.work: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series
source.locator: Prolegomena, Chapter III. Eusebius’ Church History, §1. Date of its Composition
source.quote: We are thus led to place the completion of the History in the year 324, or, to give the widest possible limits, between the latter part of 323 and the early part of 325 a.d.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: The Church History of Eusebius, which should have closed with the council of Nice, comes down only to the year 324.

events.resource: NPNF2 01 Eusebius Pamphilius Church History, Life of Constantine.epub

events.title: First Council of Nicaea
events.note: The first ecumenical council, called by Constantine, condemned Arius and confessed the Son to be of one substance (homoousios) with the Father. Its sessions closed on 25 July.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Hither, in the year 325, the twentieth of his reign (therefore the festive vicennalia), the emperor summoned the bishops of the empire

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: They closed on the 25th of July, the anniversary of the accession of Constantine

events.title: Basil the Great
events.note: Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia from 370, defender of the Nicene faith and organizer of Eastern monasticism; one of the three Cappadocian fathers.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Basil was born about the year 329, at Caesarea, the capital of Cappadocia

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: He died in 379, two years before the final victory of the Nicene orthodoxy

events.title: Constantine moves his capital to Byzantium
events.note: Constantine transferred the seat of government to Byzantium, rebuilt as Constantinople or New Rome, whose bishop later ranked next to the bishop of Rome.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Constantine, by divine command as he supposed, in the year 330, transferred the seat of his government to Byzantium

events.title: Gregory Nazianzen
events.note: Cappadocian father known as the Theologian for his five Theological Orations on the Trinity; briefly bishop of Constantinople and president of the council of 381. The source gives his death as 390 or 391.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Gregory Nazianzen was born about 330, a year before the emperor Julian

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: He died in 390 or 391; the particular circumstances of his death being now unknown.

events.title: Gregory of Nyssa
events.note: Younger brother of Basil and bishop of Nyssa from 372; a speculative theologian who defended the doctrines of the Trinity and the incarnation. His birth is dated about 335 or 336.

source.work: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series
source.locator: Prolegomena, Chapter I.—A Sketch of the Life of S. Gregory of Nyssa
source.quote: and was born most probably at Cæsarea, the capital, about a.d. 335 or 336.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: He was in Constantinople thrice afterwards, in 383, 385, and 394, and he died about the year 395.

events.title: Ambrose of Milan
events.note: Roman governor acclaimed bishop of Milan before his baptism; a preacher and hymn-writer who opposed Arianism, withstood the emperor Theodosius, and baptized Augustine.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: was born at Treves (Treviri) about 340

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: Ambrose of Milan († 397)

events.title: Jerome
events.note: Scholar and monk who spent his later life at Bethlehem, where he completed the Latin translation of the Bible known as the Vulgate.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 176. Jerome as a Divine and Scholar.
source.quote: Having already sketched the life and character of Jerome (born about 340, died in 419)

events.title: John Chrysostom
events.note: Preacher of Antioch, called Golden-mouthed, and patriarch of Constantinople from 397; deposed and exiled after offending the empress Eudoxia, he died on the way to banishment.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: He was born at Antioch, a.d. 347.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.locator: § 134. The Origenistic Controversy in Egypt and Constantinople. Theophilus and Chrysostom a.d. 399–407.
second_source.quote: On the way thither he died at Comana in Pontus, a.d. 407, in the sixtieth year of his age

events.title: Ulfilas, apostle of the Goths
events.note: Ulfilas, consecrated bishop at Constantinople, evangelized the Goths, invented the Gothic alphabet and translated the Bible into Gothic. He held Arian views, which the Gothic peoples adopted.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 21. Arian Christianity among the Goths and other German Tribes.
source.quote: The real apostle of the Goths is Ulifilas, who was consecrated bishop in 348 at Constantinople, and died there in 381, aged seventy years.

events.title: Augustine of Hippo
events.note: Bishop of Hippo in North Africa from 395 and the most influential theologian of the Western church, whose teaching on sin and grace was later taken up by the Reformers. He died during the Vandal siege of Hippo.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Aurelius Augustinus, born on the 13th of November, 354, at Tagaste

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: In the third month of the siege of Hippo, on the 28th of August, 430, in the seventy-sixth year of his age

events.title: Julian the Apostate's pagan revival
events.note: Constantine's nephew Julian renounced Christianity and tried to restore paganism in the empire during his short reign, which ended with his death in the Persian campaign.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 4. Julian the Apostate, and the Reaction of Paganism. a.d. 361–363.
source.quote: The eighteen short months of his reign Dec. 361-June 363)

events.title: Athanasius lists the New Testament canon
events.note: In his Easter letter for 367, Athanasius of Alexandria listed the books the church receives as Scripture. His New Testament comprises the twenty-seven books received today, in the older order.

source.work: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series
source.locator: Prolegomena, ch. IV. The Theology of S. Athanasius, §4. Vehicles of Revelation; Scripture, the Church, Tradition.
source.quote: The Canon of Scripture accepted by Athanasius has long been known from the fragments of the thirty-ninth Festal Letter (Easter, 367).

second_source.work: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series
second_source.locator: Festal Letters, From Letter XXXIX.—(For 367.) Of the particular books and their number, which are accepted by the Church.
second_source.quote: From Letter XXXIX.—(For 367.) Of the particular books and their number, which are accepted by the Church.

events.resource: NPNF2 04 Athanasius Select Works and Letters.epub

events.title: Basil writes On the Holy Spirit
events.note: Basil's treatise defended the full deity of the Holy Spirit, the question settled soon after at the Council of Constantinople.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: his work on the Holy Ghost, written in 375, at the request of his friend Amphilochius

events.resource: NPNF2 08 Basil Letters and Select Works.epub

events.title: Theodosius makes the Nicene faith imperial law
events.note: Soon after his accession the emperor Theodosius required all his subjects to confess the orthodox Nicene faith, making it the religion of the empire.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 122. The Final Victory of Orthodoxy, and the Council of Constantinople, 381.
source.quote: Soon after his accession he issued, in 380, the celebrated edict, in which he required all his subjects to confess the orthodox faith, and threatened the heretics with punishment.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: outwardly completed by the celebrated edict of the new emperor Theodosius, in February, 380.

events.title: First Council of Constantinople
events.note: The second ecumenical council, called by Theodosius, confirmed the Nicene faith against the Arians and adopted the Nicene Creed with an added article on the deity of the Holy Spirit.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 122. The Final Victory of Orthodoxy, and the Council of Constantinople, 381.
source.quote: Theodosius called the second ecumenical council at Constantinople in May, 381.

events.title: Jerome's Latin Vulgate
events.note: At the suggestion of Pope Damasus, Jerome revised and then translated the Latin Bible, working from the Hebrew for the Old Testament; the version became the Bible of the Western church.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Jerome began the work during his second residence in Rome (382–385), at the suggestion of pope Damasus

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: He finished the translation at Bethlehem, in the year 405, after twenty years of toil.

events.title: Augustine baptized by Ambrose
events.note: After his conversion in Milan, Augustine was baptized by Ambrose on Easter Sunday together with his friend Alypius and his son Adeodatus.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: He received baptism from Ambrose in Milan on Easter Sunday, 387, in company with his friend and fellow-convert Alypius, and his natural son Adeodatus

events.title: Rufinus's Commentary on the Apostles' Creed
events.note: Rufinus of Aquileia wrote the first Latin commentary on the baptismal creed, and with it the earliest Latin text of the old Roman creed from which the Apostles' Creed grew. Schaff says the received form came into general use in the seventh or eighth century.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: the original Roman creed, as given by Rufinus in Latin (about A.D. 390), and by Marcellus in Greek (A.D. 336–341), and the received form of the Apostles' Creed, which came into general use in the seventh or eighth century.

second_source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
second_source.quote: The first writer in the West who gives us the text of the Latin creed, with a commentary, is Rufinus, towards the close of the fourth century.

events.resource: NPNF2 03 Theodoret, Jerome, Gennadius, & Rufinus Historical Writings.epub

events.title: Council of Carthage and the canon of Scripture
events.note: Following the council of Hippo in 393, and with Augustine present, the council of Carthage fixed the list of canonical books for the church, including the Old Testament Apocrypha.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 118. Sources of Theology. Scripture and Tradition.
source.quote: The council of Hippo in 393, and the third (according to another reckoning the sixth) council of Carthage in 397, under the influence of Augustine, who attended both, fixed the catholic canon of the Holy Scriptures, including the Apocrypha of the Old Testament

events.title: Augustine writes the Confessions
events.note: Augustine's Confessions tell the story of his early life and conversion in the form of a prayer addressed to God.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Augustine composed the Confessions about the year 400.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.locator: § 152. The Augustinian System: The Primitive State of Man, and Free Will.
second_source.quote: Augustine (354–430) had already in his Confessions, in the year 400, ten years before the commencement of the Pelagian controversy

events.resource: NPNF1 01 The Confessions and Letters of St. Augustine, with a Sketch of his Life and Work.epub

events.title: Alaric sacks Rome
events.note: The Gothic king Alaric captured and plundered Rome. Pagans blamed the disaster on the abandonment of the old gods, which moved Augustine to write the City of God.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: especially the capture and sacking of the city of Rome under the Gothic king Alaric in 410

events.title: Augustine's City of God
events.note: Augustine's twenty-two books answered the pagan charge that Christianity caused Rome's fall and set out a Christian view of history as the story of two cities.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: begun in 413, after the occupation of Rome by the Gothic king Alaric, finished in 426

events.resource: NPNF1 02 St. Augustine's City of God and Christian Doctrine.epub

events.title: Council of Carthage condemns Pelagianism
events.note: More than two hundred African bishops condemned the teaching of Pelagius and Coelestius on sin and grace in canons agreeing with Augustine; Pope Zosimus soon endorsed the decision.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 149. Position of the Roman Church. Condemnation of Pelagianism.
source.quote: In a general African council held at Carthage in 418, the bishops, over two hundred in number, defined their opposition to the Pelagian errors, in eight (or nine) Canons

events.title: Council of Ephesus
events.note: The third ecumenical council, led by Cyril of Alexandria, condemned Nestorius, patriarch of Constantinople, and upheld the title Mother of God (Theotokos) for Mary.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 138. The Ecumenical Council of Ephesus, a.d. 431. The Compromise.
source.quote: Theodosius II., in connection with his Western colleague, Valentinian III., summoned a universal council on Pentecost, a.d. 431, at Ephesus

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.locator: § 138. The Ecumenical Council of Ephesus, a.d. 431. The Compromise.
second_source.quote: Cyril refused to wait, and opened the council in the church of St. Mary with a hundred and sixty bishops sixteen days after Pentecost, on the 22d of June

events.title: Pontificate of Leo the Great
events.note: Leo I, bishop of Rome, advanced the claims of the papacy, wrote the Tome adopted at Chalcedon, and persuaded Attila the Hun to spare Rome in 452.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: he was elected pope by the united voice of clergy, senate, and people, and continued in that office one-and-twenty years (440–461).

events.title: Leo's Tome to Flavian
events.note: Leo's doctrinal letter to Flavian of Constantinople set out the doctrine of two natures in one person of Christ; it was read and acclaimed at the Council of Chalcedon.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 140. The Eutychian Controversy. The Council of Robbers, a.d. 449.
source.quote: Leo, in 449, confirmed the decision of the council in several epistles, especially in a letter to Flavian

events.resource: NPNF2 12 Leo the Great, Gregory the Great.epub

events.title: Council of Chalcedon
events.note: The fourth ecumenical council confessed Christ as one person in two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation, against both Nestorius and Eutyches. It sat from 8 October to 1 November.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 141. The Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon, A.D. 451.
source.quote: The bishops assembled at Nicaea, in September, 451, but, on account of their turbulent conduct, were soon summoned to Chalcedon

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.locator: § 141. The Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon, A.D. 451.
second_source.quote: the fourth ecumenical council was opened on the 8th of October, and sat till the lst of November.

events.title: End of the Western Roman Empire
events.note: The Germanic chief Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, and ruled Italy as king.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Odoacer, who put an end to the western Roman empire in 476

events.title: Benedict of Nursia
events.note: Founder of the monastery of Monte Cassino in 529, whose Rule became the pattern for monastic life in the Western church.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Benedict was born of the illustrious house of Anicius, at Nursia (now Norcia) in Umbria, about the year 480

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: Benedict died, after partaking of the holy communion, praying, in standing posture, at the foot of the altar, on the 21st of March, 543

events.title: Baptism of Clovis
events.note: Clovis, king of the Franks, instructed by Bishop Remigius, was baptized at Reims with three thousand of his warriors; the Franks were the first Germanic people to embrace catholic rather than Arian Christianity.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 22. Conversion of Clovis and the Franks.
source.quote: On Christmas, in the year 496, he descended before the cathedral of Rheims into the baptismal basin, and three thousand of his warriors followed him as into the joys of paradise.

events.title: Council of Orange
events.note: A synod led by Caesarius of Arles condemned Semi-Pelagianism and approved Augustine's doctrine of sin and grace, though without his teaching on predestination.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 160. Victory of Semi-Augustinianism. Council of Orange, A.D. 529.
source.quote: At the synod of Orange (Arausio) in the year 529, at which Caesarius of Arles was leader, the Semi-Pelagian system, yet without mention of its adherents, was condemned in twenty-five chapters or canons

events.title: Gregory the Great
events.note: Monk, papal envoy to Constantinople, and bishop of Rome from 590 until his death, remembered as the last of the Latin fathers and the first of the medieval popes. He sent the mission that converted the Anglo-Saxons and wrote the Book of Pastoral Rule, the Moralia on Job, and the Dialogues.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Gregory was born about a.d. 540, from an old and wealthy senatorial (the Anician) family of Rome

second_source.work: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series
second_source.locator: The Book of Pastoral Rule, and Selected Epistles, of Gregory the Great: Prolegomena
second_source.quote: In the course of this indiction (on the 12th of March, a.d. 604) Gregory died.

events.title: Columbanus
events.note: Irish monk who crossed to Gaul with twelve companions and became the pioneer of the Irish missionaries on the Continent. Expelled from Burgundy in 610 for rebuking the court, he preached around Lake Zurich and Lake Constance and founded the monastery of Bobbio in Lombardy, where he died.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 23. Columbanus and the Irish Missionaries on the Continent.
source.quote: He was born in Leinster, a.d. 543, in which year St. Benedict, his celebrated monastic predecessor, died at Monte Casino

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.locator: § 23. Columbanus and the Irish Missionaries on the Continent.
second_source.quote: He died in Bobbio, Nov. 21, 615.

events.title: Second Council of Constantinople
events.note: The fifth ecumenical council, called by Justinian, condemned the Three Chapters: Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret's writings against Cyril, and the letter of Ibas, all linked with Nestorius. It sat from 5 May to 2 June.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 144. The Three, Chapters, and the Fifth Ecumenical Council, A.D. 553.
source.quote: Justinian, without the concurrence of the pope, convoked at Constantinople, a.d. 553, the Fifth Ecumenical Council, which consisted of a hundred and sixty-four bishops, and held eight sessions, from the 5th of May to the 2d of June

events.title: Columba founds the mission at Iona
events.note: The Irish monk Columba sailed with twelve companions to the island of Iona, from which he and his monks evangelized the pagan Picts of northern Scotland until his death in 597.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 18. St. Columba and the Monastery of Iona.
source.quote: In 563, the forty-second year of his age, Columba prompted by a passion for travelling and a zeal for the spread of Christianity, sailed with twelve fellow-apostles to the West of Scotland

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.locator: § 18. St. Columba and the Monastery of Iona.
second_source.quote: Saint Columba or Columbcille, (died June 9, 597) is the real apostle of Scotland.

events.title: Maximus the Confessor
events.note: Greek monk and theologian who championed the doctrine of two wills in Christ against Monotheletism. Imprisoned, scourged and mutilated for his stand, he died in exile at Lazica on the Black Sea; the Sixth Ecumenical Council later adopted the two-will doctrine he defended.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Maximus was born about 580 of a distinguished family in Constantinople

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: He was (with two of his disciples) confined in prison for several years, scourged, deprived of his tongue and right hand, and thus mutilated sent, in his old age, to Lazica in Colchis on the Pontus Euxinus, where he died of these injuries, Aug. 13, 662.

events.title: Third Council of Toledo
events.note: The Visigoths of Spain under King Reccared renounced Arianism for the catholic faith. The council gives the first clear trace of the Filioque ("and the Son") in the Nicene Creed.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: The first clear trace of the Filioque in the Nicene Creed we find at the third Council of Toledo in Spain, A.D. 589, to seal the triumph of orthodoxy over Arianism.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: which was publicly proclaimed by the Council of Toledo, May 8, 589.

events.title: Augustine's mission lands in Kent
events.note: Sent by Gregory the Great, the monk Augustine landed on the Isle of Thanet with a party of about forty. King Ethelbert of Kent was baptized, and Augustine was consecrated the first archbishop of Canterbury.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 10. The Mission of Gregory and Augustin. Conversion of Kent, a.d. 595–604.
source.quote: He started finally for England July 23d, 596, wintered in Gaul, and landed in England the following year with about forty persons, including Gallic priests and interpreters.

second_source.work: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series
second_source.locator: The Book of Pastoral Rule, and Selected Epistles, of Gregory the Great: Prolegomena
second_source.quote: The landing of the missionaries on the Isle of Thanet was, according to Bede, in the following year, a.d. 597 (H. E., I. 25, V. 24).

events.title: Muhammad's flight to Medina (the Hegira)
events.note: Muhammad and his followers fled from Mecca to Medina, where he was received as prophet and lawgiver. The flight marks the beginning of the Muslim era.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: He was forced in the year 622 to flee for his life with his followers from Mecca to Medina

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: 622. The Hegira, or the flight of Mohammed from Mecca to Medina. Beginning of the Mohammedan era.

events.title: Caliph Omar captures Jerusalem
events.note: Jerusalem fell to the Arab armies under the second caliph during the conquest of Palestine, Syria and Egypt, which brought the patriarchates of Jerusalem, Antioch and Alexandria under Muslim rule.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: 636. Capture of Jerusalem by the Caliph Omar.

events.title: Synod of Whitby
events.note: Before King Oswy of Northumbria, Colman defended the Irish (Scottish) reckoning of Easter and Wilfrid the Roman. The king decided for Rome, and the Northumbrian church conformed to Roman observance.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 13. Conformity to Row Established. Wilfrid, Theodore, Bede.
source.quote: The controversy was decided in a Synod held at Whitby in 664 in the presence of King Oswy or Oswio and his son Alfrid.

events.title: The Venerable Bede
events.note: Monk of Wearmouth and Jarrow, the first native English scholar and the father of English church history. His Ecclesiastical History of England is the chief source for the English church to the eighth century; he died while translating the Gospel of John into Anglo-Saxon.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: He was born in 673, probably in the village of Jarrow, on the south bank of the Tyne, Northumbria, near the Scottish border.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: He died on Wednesday, May 26, 735, of a complaint accompanied with asthma, from which he had long suffered.

events.title: Boniface, apostle of Germany
events.note: English missionary (Winfried) who evangelized Hesse and Thuringia, felled the sacred oak at Geismar, organized the German church under Rome, and became archbishop of Mainz. He was killed by pagans in Friesland; Schaff gives the year as 754 or 755, the New Schaff-Herzog as 755.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: He was born about 680 from a noble family, at Kirton in Wessex the last stronghold of paganism among the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms.

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.quote: BONIFACE, SAINT: The apostle of the Germans; b. at Crediton (8 m. n.w. of Exeter), Devonshire, between 675 and 683; d. a martyr on the banks of the Borne near Dokkum (13 m. n.e. of Leeuwarden), in Friesland, June 5, 755.

events.title: Third Council of Constantinople
events.note: The Sixth Ecumenical Council, meeting in the imperial palace, defined that Christ has two wills, divine and human, and condemned Monotheletism. Among those it condemned as Monothelete heretics was Pope Honorius I.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: It convened in the imperial palace at Constantinople, and held eighteen sessions from Nov. 7, 680, to Sept. 16, 681.

events.title: Emperor Leo III begins the war on images
events.note: The Byzantine emperor Leo the Isaurian first prohibited the worship of images and in a second edict (730) ordered their removal, opening the iconoclastic controversy. John of Damascus wrote in reply in defense of images.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 101. The Iconoclastic War, and the Synod of 754.
source.quote: Then, in the tenth year (726), he began his war upon the images.

events.title: Battle of Tours
events.note: Charles Martel defeated the Arab army of Abd-er-Rahman between Poitiers and Tours, checking the Muslim advance into western Europe.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: the defeat of Abd-er Rahman by Charles Martel between Poitiers and Tours in 732—one hundred and ten years after the Hegira—checked their progress in the West

events.title: Alcuin of York
events.note: Northumbrian scholar trained at the cathedral school of York who became Charlemagne's chief adviser in church and learning. He revised the Latin Vulgate, wrote against Adoptionism, and spent his last years at the monastery of St. Martin at Tours.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Flaccus Albinus, or, as he is commonly called in the Old English form, Alcuin (“friend of the temple”), the ecclesiastical prime minister of Charlemagne, was born in Yorkshire about 735.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: It is remarkable that he died upon the anniversary on which he had desired to die, the Festival of Pentecost, May 19, 804.

events.title: John of Damascus writes the Fount of Knowledge
events.note: The last of the Greek fathers summed up Greek theology in the Fount of Knowledge, whose third and longest part is the accurate summary of the Orthodox Faith (the Exposition of the Orthodox Faith). Schaff dates it after 743, the year Cosmas, to whom it is dedicated, became bishop; John died probably in 754.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: It is dedicated to Cosmas, bishop of Maiuma, his foster-brother and fellow-student under the old monk. Its date is after 743, the year of Cosmas’s consecration.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: He died at St. Sabas; the exact date is not known, probably 754.

events.resource: NPNF2 09 Hilary of Poitiers, John of Damascus.epub

events.title: The Donation of Pepin
events.note: Pepin, king of the Franks, defeated the Lombards and gave the conquered Exarchate of Ravenna and the Pentapolis to the pope. Schaff calls this gift the foundation of the Patrimony of St. Peter, the pope's temporal power.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 55. Alliance of the Papacy with the New Monarchy of the Franks. Pepin and the Patrimony of St. Peter. a.d. 741–755.
source.quote: Pepin crossed the Alps again with his army, defeated the Lombards, and bestowed the conquered territory upon the pope (755).

events.title: Second Council of Nicaea
events.note: The Seventh Ecumenical Council, convened by the Empress Irene and presided over by the patriarch Tarasius, set aside the iconoclastic synod of 754 and sanctioned the veneration of images. The Frankish church rejected it at Frankfort in 794.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 102. The Restoration of Image-Worship by the Seventh Oecumenical Council, 787.
source.quote: Irene convened the seventh oecumenical council in the year 787, at Nicaea, which was less liable to iconoclastic disturbances than Constantinople, yet within easy reach of the court

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.locator: § 102. The Restoration of Image-Worship by the Seventh Oecumenical Council, 787.
second_source.quote: It was attended by about three hundred and fifty bishops, under the presidency of Tarasius, and held only eight sessions from September 24 to October 23

events.title: Synod of Frankfort
events.note: Charlemagne's synod of the Frankish and German churches endorsed the Caroline Books, condemned the worship of images, and rejected the Second Council of Nicaea. It also condemned the Adoptionism of Felix of Urgel and Elipandus of Toledo.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 104. The Caroline Books and the Frankish Church on Image-Worship.
source.quote: A Synod in Frankfort, a.d. 794, the most important held during the reign of Charlemagne, and representing the churches of France and Germany, in the presence of two papal legates (Theophylactus and Stephanus), endorsed the doctrine of the Libri Carolini

events.title: Charlemagne crowned emperor
events.note: At Christmas in St. Peter's, Rome, Pope Leo III crowned Charles, king of the Franks, as emperor. Schaff treats the act as the founding of the Holy Roman Empire.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 57. Founding of the Holy Roman Empire, a.d. 800. Charlemagne and Leo III
source.quote: While Charles was celebrating Christmas in St. Peter’s, in the year of our Lord 800, and kneeling in prayer before the altar, the pope, as under a sudden inspiration (but no doubt in consequence of a premeditated scheme), placed a golden crown upon his head

events.title: Ansgar, apostle of the North
events.note: Frankish monk of Corbie who began the mission to Denmark in 827, preached in Sweden, and became archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen. He built the first church in Denmark, at Hedeby.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 29. The Christianization of Denmark. St. Ansgar.
source.quote: Ansgar was born about 800 (according to general acceptation Sept. 9, 801) in the diocese of Amiens, of Frankish parents, and educated in the abbey of Corbie, under the guidance of Adalhard.

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.quote: ANSGAR or ANSKAR (Aasgejr, Osgejr, “God’s Spear"; the modern Oscar): The apostle of Scandinavia, first archbishop of Hamburg (831-865); b. of prominent Frankish parents near the monastery of Corbie (9 m. e. of Amiens), probably in 801; d. at Bremen Feb. 3, 865.

events.title: Synod of Aix requires priests to learn the creeds
events.note: A Frankish synod at Aix-la-Chapelle required priests to learn the Athanasian and Apostles' Creeds and the Lord's Prayer. Schaff places the first appearance of the Athanasian Creed in France shortly before or during the age of Charlemagne.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: A Synod of Aix, 802, prescribed that they should learn the Athanasian and Apostles’ Creed, the Lord’s Prayer with exposition

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.locator: § 107. The Controversy on the Procession of the Holy Spirit.
second_source.quote: It was expressed in the so-called Athanasian Creed, which made its appearance in France shortly before or during the age of Charlemagne.

events.title: Radbertus writes On the Body and Blood of the Lord
events.note: Paschasius Radbertus, monk and later abbot of Corbie, taught that the bread and wine are changed into the flesh and blood of Christ; Schaff counts him the first to teach transubstantiation clearly. His fellow monk Ratramnus replied at the request of Charles the Bald with a spiritual view of the Supper.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: He wrote a book “on the Body and Blood of the Lord,” composed for his disciple Placidus of New Corbie in the year 831, and afterwards reedited it in a more popular form, and dedicated it to the Emperor Charles the Bald, as a Christmas gift (844).

events.title: Images restored: the first Sunday of Orthodoxy
events.note: Under the regent Theodora a synod at Constantinople restored the veneration of images and anathematized the iconoclasts, ending the controversy in the East. The day is kept in the Eastern church as the Sunday of Orthodoxy.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 103. Iconoclastic Reaction, and Final Triumph of Image-Worship, a.d. 842.
source.quote: On the 19th of February, 842, the images were again introduced into the churches of Constantinople. It was the first celebration of the “Sunday of Orthodoxy,”

events.title: The Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals
events.note: A Frankish collection of church law that mixed genuine canons with forged decretal letters of the early bishops of Rome, meant to protect the clergy against the secular power by securing to the pope the final sentence in the trials of bishops. It was accepted as genuine through the Middle Ages; Schaff dates its compilation between 847 and 865 (or 857), and it was first cited by a synod at Chiersy in 857.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The authorship must be assigned to some ecclesiastic of the Frankish church, probably of the diocese of Rheims, between 847 and 865 (or 857), but scholars differ as to the writer.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: he is first quoted by a French Synod at Chiersy in 857, and then by Hincmar of Rheims repeatedly since 859.

events.title: Gottschalk condemned for double predestination
events.note: The monk Gottschalk of Orbais taught, from Augustine, a twofold predestination of the elect to life and the reprobate to death. The Synod of Mainz (848) condemned him, and the Synod of Chiersy (849) deposed him, had him scourged, and imprisoned him until his death.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: He appeared before a Synod at Mainz, which was opened Oct. 1, 848, in the presence of the German king, and boldly professed his belief in a two-fold predestination, to life and to death

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: Gottschalk was summoned before a synod of Chiersy (in palatio Carisiaco) in the spring of 849. He refused to recant, and was condemned as an incorrigible heretic, deposed from the priesthood, publicly scourged for obstinacy

events.title: Cyril and Methodius go to Moravia
events.note: The brothers Cyril (Constantine) and Methodius of Thessalonica, apostles of the Slavs, came to Moravia at the invitation of Prince Rastislaw and used the Slavic language in worship. Methodius was later consecrated archbishop for the region.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 34. Cyrillus and Methodius, the Apostles of the Slavs. Christianization of Moravia, Bohemia and Poland.
source.quote: He afterward labored among the Bulgarians and finally went, in company with his brother, to Moravia, on the invitation of Rastislaw, in 863.

events.title: The Photian schism
events.note: Pope Nicolas I declared Photius deposed as patriarch of Constantinople in favor of Ignatius; Photius answered with a synod deposing the pope and an encyclical charging the Western church with adding the Filioque to the Nicene Creed. It was the first serious outbreak of the conflict that later divided the Eastern and Western churches.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 70. The Patriarch and the Pope. Photius and Nicolas.
source.quote: Nicolas, in a Roman Synod (863), decided in favor of the innocent Ignatius, and pronounced sentence of deposition against Photius with a threat of excommunication in case of disobedience.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.locator: § 70. The Patriarch and the Pope. Photius and Nicolas.
second_source.quote: Photius, enraged by this conduct and the Bulgarian interference, held a counter-synod, and deposed in turn the successor of St. Peter (867).

events.title: Founding of Cluny Abbey
events.note: Duke William of Aquitaine founded the abbey of Cluny under the Rule of St. Benedict. Its abbots led a reform of monastic life and later of the papacy and the wider church.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: It was founded by the pious Duke William of Aquitania in 910, to the honor of St. Peter and St. Paul, on the basis of the rule of St. Benedict.

events.title: Baptism of Vladimir of Kiev
events.note: The grand duke Vladimir of Kiev, grandson of Olga, was baptized on the day of his marriage to the Byzantine princess Anne and established Christianity of the Greek rite as the religion of the Russians.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: He married Anne, and was baptized on the day of his wedding, a.d. 988.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: The progress of Christianity among the Russians was slow until the grand-duke Vladimir (980–1015), a grandson of Olga, and revered as Isapostolos (“Equal to an Apostle”) with one sweep established it as the religion of the country.

events.title: Anselm of Canterbury
events.note: Abbot of Bec and from 1093 archbishop of Canterbury, Anselm is reckoned the first of the great Schoolmen. His Proslogium set out the ontological argument for God's existence and his Cur Deus homo a satisfaction theory of the atonement.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Anselm of Canterbury, 1033–1109, the first of the great Schoolmen, was one of the ablest and purest men of the mediaeval Church.

events.title: Synod of Sutri
events.note: On his way to Rome for his coronation, King Henry III held a synod at Sutri and, a few days later, another at Rome; together they deposed the three rival claimants to the papacy. Suidger of Bamberg was then installed as Clement II.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 66. Henry III and the Synod of Sutri. Deposition of three rival Popes. a.d. 1046.
source.quote: On his way to Rome for the coronation he held (Dec. 20, 1046) a synod at Sutri, a small town about twenty-five miles north of Rome, and a few days afterwards another synod at Rome which completed the work.

events.title: Schism of East and West
events.note: Legates of Pope Leo IX laid a sentence of excommunication against Patriarch Michael Cerularius on the altar of Hagia Sophia, and the patriarch answered with a synodical counter-anathema. Schaff treats this as the completion of the schism between the Greek and Latin churches.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 71. Progress and Completion of the Schism. Cerularius.
source.quote: Finally, on the 16th of July, 1054, they excommunicated the patriarch and all those who should persistently censure the faith of the church of Rome or its mode of offering the holy sacrifice.

events.title: Berengar made to recant at Rome
events.note: Berengar of Tours taught a spiritual rather than a bodily eating of Christ in the Lord's Supper. At a Lateran council under Nicholas II, Cardinal Humbert forced a formula of recantation on him, which he accepted on his knees before throwing his books into the fire; a Lateran council under Gregory VII required another recantation of him in 1079.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Berengar appeared before a Lateran council held in 1059, under Nicolas II., but was bitterly disappointed.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: A Lateran Council in February, 1079, required Berengar to sign a formula which affirmed the conversion of substance in terms that cut off all sophistical escape.

events.title: Pontificate of Gregory VII (Hildebrand)
events.note: Hildebrand, for many years the leading counsellor of the popes, was elected pope as Gregory VII. His reign enforced clerical celibacy, forbade lay investiture and brought the papacy into open conflict with the German king Henry IV.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The world has had few rulers equal to Gregory VII. 1073–1085, Alexander III. 1159–1181, and Innocent III. 1198–1216

events.title: Henry IV's penance at Canossa
events.note: Under the ban of Gregory VII, the German king Henry IV stood for three days as a barefoot penitent in the castle court at Canossa before the pope admitted and absolved him.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: For three days, from the 25th to the 28th of January, he stood in the court between the inner walls, as a penitent suppliant, with bare head and feet

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: Henry arrived at the foot of the castle-steep, Jan. 21, 1077, when the cold was severe and the ground covered with snow.

events.title: Peter Abelard
events.note: A brilliant and controversial teacher at Paris, Abelard was arraigned by Bernard of Clairvaux at the synod of Sens in 1141 and appealed to Rome, where Innocent II condemned him as a heretic. He spent his last days at Cluny under the protection of Peter the Venerable.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: During the first half of the twelfth century, Peter Abaelard, 1079–1142, was one of the most conspicuous characters of Europe.

events.title: Bernard of Clairvaux
events.note: Bernard entered the Cistercian order in 1113 and founded the abbey of Clairvaux in 1115. A preacher, mystic and adviser of popes, he was admired by both Luther and Calvin.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: St. Bernard, 1090–1153, founder and abbot of the convent of Clairvaux, was the model monk of the Middle Ages

events.title: Council of Clermont calls the First Crusade
events.note: Pope Urban II addressed a great crowd at the council of Clermont in southern France and called for an expedition to recover Jerusalem. Peter the Hermit became the movement's chief popular preacher.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The call which resulted in the first expedition for the recovery of Jerusalem was made by Pope Urban II. at the Council of Clermont, 1095.
