events.title: Anselm completes Cur Deus Homo
events.note: Anselm's dialogue "Why God Became Man" explains Christ's death as the satisfaction due to God's injured honor. It was begun in England and finished in Apulia during his exile.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: the last was begun in England “in great tribulation of heart,” and finished at Schiavi, a mountain village of Apulia, where Anselm enjoyed a few months of rest in 1098.

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.quote: was first given scientific statement by Anselm (q.v.) in his Cur Deus homo (1098)

events.title: Crusaders capture Jerusalem
events.note: The First Crusade ended with the storming of Jerusalem and the founding of a Latin kingdom, which held the city until 1187.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 50. The First Crusade and the Capture of Jerusalem.
source.quote: The culmination of the First Crusade was the fall of Jerusalem, July 15, 1099.

events.title: Concordat of Worms
events.note: Pope Calixtus II and Emperor Henry V settled the investiture controversy by compromise: the Church invested bishops with ring and crosier, while the emperor conferred their temporal holdings with the sceptre.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The Concordat of Worms was signed, Sept. 23, 1122.

events.title: Otto of Bamberg's mission to Pomerania
events.note: Bishop Otto of Bamberg, called the Apostle of Pomerania, preached among the Pomeranians with the blessing of Pope Honorius II and made a second tour there in 1128.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Bernard was followed by Otto, bishop of Bamberg, 1102–1139, who made his first tour at Bernard’s instance. He won the title of Apostle of Pommerania. In 1124 he set his face towards the country, furnished with the blessing of Honorius II.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: In 1128 Otto made a second tour to Pommerania.

events.title: Murder of Thomas Becket
events.note: Archbishop Thomas Becket of Canterbury, who had resisted Henry II over the rights of the Church, was killed in his cathedral by four knights of the king's household. He was canonized soon afterward.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: b. in London between 1110 and 1120; assassinated at Canterbury Dec. 29, 1170.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.locator: § 33. The Martyrdom of Thomas Becket. Dec. 29, 1170.
second_source.quote: reached St. Augustine’s abbey outside of the walls of Canterbury, early on the 29th of December, which was a Tuesday.

events.title: Dominic
events.note: A Spanish canon who preached against the Albigenses in southern France, Dominic founded the Order of Preachers, whose members later became the chief agents of the Inquisition.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Domingo, or Dominic, was born 1170 at Calaroga, Spain,

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: He died, lying on ashes, at Bologna, Aug. 6, 1221, and lies buried there in the convent of St. Nicholas

events.title: Peter Waldo gives away his goods
events.note: Waldo, a merchant of Lyons, gave his property to the poor, had the Gospels translated into the common tongue and began preaching; his followers, the Poor Men of Lyons, became the Waldenses.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Waldo renounced his property, sent his two daughters to the convent of Fontevrault, gave his wife a portion of his goods, and distributed the remainder to the poor. This was about 1170.

events.title: Robert Grosseteste
events.note: Bishop of Lincoln from 1235, Grosseteste reformed clerical and monastic abuses and refused to install the pope's nephew in an English living. Schaff calls him a forerunner of Wyclif in his use of the Scriptures.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Robert Grosseteste, 1175–1253, had a wider range of influence than Hugh, and was probably the most noteworthy Englishman of his generation.

events.title: Francis of Assisi
events.note: The son of a cloth merchant of Assisi, Francis broke with his father for a life of poverty and preaching and founded the Franciscan order of friars. In 1219 he preached in Egypt and Syria.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Francesco,—Francis,—Bernardone, 1182–1226, was born and died in Assisi.

events.title: Synod of Verona condemns the Waldenses
events.note: The synod held under Pope Lucius III anathematized the Poor Men of Lyons for preaching without the bishops' consent, classing them with the Cathari, and passed a decree on the trial and punishment of heretics.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The synod of Verona, 1184, designated them as "Humiliati, or Poor Men of Lyons," and anathematized them, putting them into the same category with the Cathari and Patarines.

events.title: Saladin takes Jerusalem
events.note: Saladin captured Jerusalem after a siege, ending the Latin kingdom's hold on the city. Its loss prompted the Third Crusade.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: On Oct. 2, 1187, Saladin entered Jerusalem after it had made a brave resistance.

events.title: Pontificate of Innocent III
events.note: Schaff calls Innocent III's reign the golden age of the medieval papacy. He placed England under interdict, launched crusades against the Albigenses and presided over the Fourth Lateran Council.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The brilliant pontificate of Innocent III., 1198–1216, lasted as long as the combined and uneventful reigns of his five predecessors

events.title: Royal privilege for the University of Paris
events.note: King Philip Augustus of France gave the masters and students of Paris rights independent of the city government. Paris became the chief seat of theological learning in the West until the Reformation.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: In the year 1200 Philip Augustus, king of France, conferred upon it a valuable privilege, granting the students and teaching body independent rights over against the municipal government.

events.title: Fourth Crusade takes Constantinople
events.note: Crusaders and Venetians stormed and plundered Constantinople and set up a Latin empire that lasted until 1261, deepening the breach between the Greek and Latin churches.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 55. The Fourth Crusade and the Capture of Constantinople. 1200–1204.
source.quote: The confusion within the palace and the failure to pay the promised reward were a sufficient excuse for the invaders to assault the city, which fell April 12, 1204.

events.title: Fourth Lateran Council
events.note: Innocent III's great council defined transubstantiation as the doctrine of the Church and set up the Inquisition against heretics. Its three sittings were attended by 412 bishops and 800 abbots and priors.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The council was held in the Lateran and had three sittings, Nov. 11, 20, 30, 1215.

events.title: Bonaventure
events.note: Called the Seraphic Doctor, Bonaventure taught at Paris, became general of the Franciscan order in 1257 and wrote its authorized life of Francis. He died during the Second Council of Lyons.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Bonaventura 1221–1274, called the Seraphic doctor,—doctor seraphicus,—was born in Tuscany.

events.title: Thomas Aquinas
events.note: A Dominican taught by Albertus Magnus, Aquinas organized scholastic theology into a complete system in his Summa theologica, which he left unfinished. He died on his way to the Second Council of Lyons.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Thomas Aquinas, called the Angelic doctor,—doctor angelicus, — 1225–1274, is the prince of the Schoolmen

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: He died on his way to the oecumenical council of Lyons, March 7, 1274, only forty-eight years of age,

events.title: Synod of Toulouse forbids laymen the Bible
events.note: Meeting at the close of the Albigensian crusades, the synod completed the code of the Inquisition and forbade laymen to possess the Bible.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The synod of Toulouse, 1229, presided over by the papal legate, celebrated the close of the Albigensian crusades and perfected the code of the Inquisition. It has an unenviable distinction among the great synods on account of its decree forbidding laymen to have the Bible in their possession.

events.title: First Council of Lyons
events.note: Pope Innocent IV's council, reckoned by the Latins the thirteenth ecumenical council, excommunicated and deposed the emperor Frederick II.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 44. The First Council of Lyons and the Close of Frederick’s Career. 1241–1250.
source.quote: It is known as the First Council of Lyons, or the Thirteenth Oecumenical Council, and met in Lyons, 1245.

events.title: Dante Alighieri
events.note: Florentine poet whose Divine Comedy, conceived in 1300, gives a poetic view of the moral universe. His De monarchia argued for the independence of the civil power from the papacy.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Dante Alighieri, 1265–1321, the first of Italian and the greatest of mediaeval poets, has given us in his Divina Commedia, the Divine Comedy, conceived in 1300, a poetic view of the moral universe under the aspect of eternity

events.title: Second Council of Lyons
events.note: Summoned by Gregory X, the council received Greek delegates who accepted the Latin creed and papal primacy on behalf of the emperor Michael Palaeologus, but the Greek clergy rejected the union.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: 6. The Second council of Lyons or the Fourteenth oecumenical, 1274, was summoned by Gregory X., and attended by five hundred bishops and one thousand other ecclesiastics.

events.title: Thomas Bradwardine
events.note: English theologian called the Profound Doctor, whose De causa Dei contra Pelagium defended the priority of God's grace and acknowledged Augustine as his master. He was consecrated archbishop of Canterbury in 1349 and died a few weeks later.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: BRADWARDINE, THOMAS: Archbishop of Canterbury; b. probably at Chichester, Sussex, 1290; d. in London Aug. 28, 1349.

events.title: Fall of Acre
events.note: The surrender of Acre, the last stronghold of the crusaders in Palestine, ended the Latin presence there.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 58. The Last Stronghold of the Crusaders in Palestine.
source.quote: In 1289 Tripoli was lost, and the bitter rivalry between the Military Orders hastened the surrender of Acre, 1291

events.title: Boniface VIII proclaims a Jubilee Year
events.note: Boniface VIII's bull promised full remission to penitents who visited St. Peter's in Rome during the year 1300. It seems to have been the first Jubilee of its kind.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: An important and picturesque event of Boniface’s pontificate was the Jubilee Year, celebrated in 1300.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: Interesting as the story is, the Jubilee celebration of 1300 seems to have been the first of its kind. Boniface’s bull, appointing it, promised full remission to all, being penitent and confessing their sins, who should visit St. Peter’s during the year 1300.

events.title: Boniface VIII issues the bull Unam Sanctam
events.note: Issued against Philip the Fair of France, the bull declared that subjection to the Roman pontiff is necessary to salvation. The Fifth Lateran Council reaffirmed it in 1516.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 4. Boniface VIII. and Philip the Fair of France.
source.quote: The great importance of Boniface’s bull, Unam Sanctam, issued against Philip the Fair, Nov. 18, 1302, justifies its reproduction both in translation and the original Latin.

events.title: The papacy at Avignon (the Babylonian Captivity)
events.note: Clement V made Avignon the papal residence, and seven French popes lived there in what was called the Babylonian Captivity of the papacy. Gregory XI returned the papal court to Rome in 1377.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 6. The Transfer of the Papacy to Avignon.
source.quote: After holding his court at Bordeaux, Poictiers, and Toulouse, he chose, in 1309, Avignon as his residence.

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.quote: Seven popes resided there,—Clement V, John XXII, Benedict XII, Clement VI, Innocent VI, Urban V, and Gregory XI; and during this period (1309-77; the so-called Babylonian Captivity of the popes) it was a gay and corrupt city.

events.title: John Wycliffe
events.note: Oxford theologian called the Morning Star of the Reformation. He asserted the supreme authority of Scripture, rejected transubstantiation and sent out itinerant 'poor priests'; the Council of Constance later condemned his memory and ordered his bones exhumed.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: John Wyclif, called the Morning Star of the Reformation, and, at the time of his death, in England and in Bohemia the Evangelical doctor, was born about 1324 near the village of Wyclif, Yorkshire, in the diocese of Durham.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: While saying mass in his church, he was struck again with paralysis, and passed away two or three days after, Dec. 29, 1384, "having lit a fire which shall never be put out."

events.title: Gerrit Groote
events.note: Dutch preacher of Deventer whose followers formed the Brothers of the Common Life and the Windesheim Congregation, a movement of practical devotion, copying and schooling in the Low Countries.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 34. Gerrit de Groote and the Brothers of the Common Life.
source.quote: under the leadership of Gerrit Groote, 1340–1384, and Florentius Radewyn, 1350–1400, who had finished his studies in Prag. They were the founders of the Windesheim Congregation and the genial company known as the Brothers of the Common Life

events.title: The Black Death
events.note: A plague swept over Europe from Hungary to Scotland and from Spain to Sweden. The clergy died in great numbers, and in England about half the population is estimated to have perished.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: During Clement’s pontificate, 1348–1349, the Black Death swept over Europe from Hungary to Scotland and from Spain to Sweden, one of the most awful and mysterious scourges that has ever visited mankind.

events.title: John Hus
events.note: Bohemian preacher at Prague who took up Wycliffe's teaching. Summoned to the Council of Constance under a safe-conduct from Sigismund, he was condemned and burned at the stake.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: John Huss was born of Czech parents, 1369, at Husinec in Southern Bohemia.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: Among the more prominent individual cases of persecution, we may mention the burning of Hus (1415) and Jerome of Prague (1416) by order of the Council of Constance, the burning of Savonarola in Florence (1498)

events.title: The Great Western Schism
events.note: After the disputed election of Urban VI, the French cardinals chose Clement VII at Fondi, and rival popes reigned at Rome and Avignon. The schism ended when the Council of Constance elected Martin V on November 11, 1417.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Retiring to Fondi, in Neapolitan territory, the French cardinals proceeded to a new eIection, Sept. 20, 1378, the choice falling upon one of their number, Robert of Geneva, the son of Amadeus, count of Geneva.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: The papal vacancy was filled, Nov. 11, 1417, by the election of Cardinal Oddo Colonna, who took the name of Martin V.

events.title: Thomas à Kempis
events.note: Monk of the Augustinian convent of Mount St. Agnes near Zwolle, schooled by the Brothers of the Common Life at Deventer. The Imitation of Christ is generally ascribed to him.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 35. The Imitation of Christ. Thomas à Kempis.
source.quote: The author, Thomas à Kempis, 1380–1471, was born in Kempen, a town 40 miles northwest of Cologne, and died at Zwolle, in the Netherlands.

events.title: Wycliffe's English Bible
events.note: The first Bible in English, translated from the Latin Vulgate by Wycliffe with Nicholas Hereford and revised after his death by John Purvey. The years are those its editors, Forshall and Madden, assign to the two versions.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: A manuscript preserved in the Bodleian, Forshall and Madden affirm to be without question the original copy of Hereford himself. These editors place the dates of the versions in 1382 and 1388.

events.title: England passes an act for burning heretics
events.note: Parliament under Henry IV passed the first English statute for the burning of heretics, aimed at the Lollards, the followers of Wycliffe. It forbade them to preach, hold schools or issue books.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: With the accession of Henry IV. of Lancaster (1399–1413), a severe policy was adopted. The culminating point of legislation was reached in 1401, when parliament passed the act for the burning of heretics, the first act of the kind in England.

events.title: Council of Pisa
events.note: The first of the reformatory councils condemned both rival popes, Gregory XII and Benedict XIII, and its cardinals elected Alexander V. Neither of the condemned popes yielded, so the council opened with two popes and closed with three.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The three councils of Pisa, 1409, Constance, 1414, and Basel, 1431, of which the schism was the occasion, are known in history as the Reformatory councils.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: At the opening of the Pisan synod there were two popes; at its close, three.

events.title: Council of Constance
events.note: Called by John XXIII and Sigismund, the council declared its own authority as a general council, ended the schism by electing Martin V, and condemned John Hus and Jerome of Prague.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The council, which was appointed for Nov. 1, 1414, lasted nearly four years, and proved to be one of the most imposing gatherings which has ever convened in Western Europe.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: On completing its forty-fifth session it was adjourned by Martin, April 22, 1418.

events.title: Jerome of Prague burned at Constance
events.note: A year after Hus's death, his friend Jerome of Prague, who shared his enthusiasm for Wycliffe, was condemned by the Council of Constance and burned on the spot where Hus had suffered.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: A year after Huss’ martyrdom, on May 30, 1416, his friend Jerome of Prag was condemned by the council and also suffered at the stake.

events.title: Wessel Gansfort
events.note: Dutch theologian of Groningen whose teaching anticipated the Reformers. Luther wrote that if he had read Wessel earlier, his enemies might have said Luther drew everything from Wessel.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: A still nearer approach to the views of the Reformers was made by Wessel Gansfort, commonly called John Wessel, born in Groningen, 1420, died 1489.

events.title: Council of Basel
events.note: The last of the reformatory councils asserted conciliar authority against Eugenius IV and negotiated the Compacts granting the Hussites the cup. It moved to Lausanne in 1448 and dissolved in 1449.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: On the day set for the opening of the council in Basel, March 7, 1431, only a single prelate was present, the abbot of Vezelay. The formal opening occurred July 23

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: In June, 1448, it adjourned to Lausanne. Reduced to a handful of adherents, and weary of being a synonym for innocuous failure, it voted to accept Nicolas V., Eugenius’ successor, as legitimate pope, and then quietly breathed its last, April 25, 1449.

events.title: Council of Ferrara-Florence
events.note: The Greek emperor and patriarch attended, and articles of union with Rome were publicly read at Florence on July 6, 1439. The union was rejected in Constantinople.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: In the meantime the council at Ferrara had been opened, Jan. 8, 1438, and was daily gaining adherents.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: On Aug. 7, 1445, Eugenius adjourned the long council which had begun its sittings at Basel, continued them at Ferrara and Florence, and concluded them in the Lateran.

events.title: Girolamo Savonarola
events.note: Prior of the Dominican convent of St. Mark's in Florence, whose preaching sought a moral reform of the city. He was condemned and put to death in Florence.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Savonarola, born in Ferrara Sept. 21, 1452, died in Florence May 23, 1498, was the third of seven children.

events.title: Fall of Constantinople
events.note: The Ottoman Turks took Constantinople, ending the Byzantine empire. The last emperor died in the siege, and the church of St. Sophia was turned into a mosque.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Scarcely in any pontificate has so notable and long-forecasted an event occurred as the fall of Constantinople into the hands of the Turks, which took place May 29, 1453.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible printed at Mainz
events.note: The first printed Latin Bible, issued at Mainz in two volumes without a date; Schaff places it before 1455. It is also called the Mazarin Bible.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 77. The Study and Circulation of the Bible.
source.quote: The first printed Latin Bible, which appeared at Mainz without date and in two volumes, belongs before 1455 and bears the name of the Gutenberg Bible from the printer or the Mazarin Bible from the copy which was found in the library of Cardinal Mazarin.

events.title: The Bohemian Brethren (Unitas Fratrum) appear
events.note: The third outgrowth of the Hussite movement, the Unitas Fratrum continued to grow until the time of the Reformation. The body still exists in the Moravians.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Its beginnings are uncertain. It appears distinctly for the first time in 1457, and continued to grow till the time of the Reformation.

events.title: Sixtus IV sanctions the Spanish Inquisition
events.note: The bull authorized Ferdinand and Isabella to appoint inquisitors and to remove and replace them as they saw fit. The tribunal was constituted at Seville in 1480, directed first against converted Jews suspected of keeping Jewish practices in secret.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Sixtus IV., who was then occupying the chair of St. Peter, did not hesitate in a matter so important, and on Nov. 1, 1478, issued the bull sanctioning the fell Spanish tribunal.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: After a delay of two years, the commission was constituted, 1480, and consisted of two Dominican theologians, Michael de Morillo and John of St. Martin, and a friar of St. Pablo, Seville.

events.title: Martin Luther
events.note: Augustinian monk and Wittenberg professor whose theses on indulgences opened the German Reformation. He was born and died at Eisleben.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Martin Luther was born Nov. 10, 1483, an hour before midnight, at Eisleben in Prussian Saxony, where he died, Feb. 18, 1546.

events.title: William Tyndale
events.note: English translator of the Bible from the original languages. Working in hiding on the Continent, he was arrested at Antwerp, then strangled and burned at Vilvoorden.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: Biblical translator and martyr; b. most probably at North Nibley (15 m. s.s.w. of Gloucester), England, in 1484; d. at Vilvoorden (6 m. n.e. of Brussels), Belgium, Oct. 6, 1536.

events.title: Ulrich Zwingli
events.note: Swiss Reformer who led the Reformation at Zurich from 1519. He was killed at the battle of Kappel.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Huldreich or Ulrich Zwingli was born January 1, 1484, seven weeks after Luther, in a lowly shepherd’s cottage at Wildhaus in the county of Toggenburg, now belonging to the Canton St. Gall.

second_source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
second_source.quote: Zwingli (1484–1531) represents the first stage of the Reformed Church in Switzerland.

events.title: Thomas Cranmer
events.note: First Protestant archbishop of Canterbury and chief author of the English Prayer Book and the Forty-two Articles. He was burned at Oxford under Queen Mary.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: CRANMER, THOMAS: The first Protestant archbishop of Canterbury; b. at Aslacton (9 m. e. of Nottingham), Nottinghamshire, July 2, 1489; d. at Oxford Mar. 21, 1556.

events.title: William Farel
events.note: French evangelist who brought the Reformation to Neuchâtel and Geneva and in 1536 persuaded Calvin to stay in Geneva. He spent his last years as pastor at Neuchâtel.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Guillaume Farel, the oldest of seven children of a poor but noble family, was born in the year 1489 (five years after Luther and Zwingli, twenty years before Calvin) at Gap

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: Soon after his return to Neuchâtel, he died peacefully, Sept. 13, 1565, seventy-six years old.

events.title: Martin Bucer
events.note: Reformer of Strassburg, who worked to reconcile Luther and Zwingli on the Lord's Supper. After the Schmalkald War he went to England, and from 1550 until his death he lectured at Cambridge.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.locator: Butzer, Martin, 1. Early Activity in the Protestant Cause
source.quote: Martin Butzer (Bucer) was born at Schlettstadt (26 m. s.w. of Strasburg) Nov. 11, 1491; d. at Cambridge, Eng., Feb. 28, 1551.

events.title: Philip Melanchthon
events.note: German humanist and Reformer, Luther's colleague at Wittenberg, and author of the Augsburg Confession and its Apology.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: Philipp Melanchthon, the German humanist and Reformer, was born at Bretten (13 m. e.n.e. of Carlsruhe) Feb. 16, 1497, and died at Wittenberg Apr. 19, 1560.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: On the 19th of April, 1560, Melanchthon was delivered from "the fury of the theologians" and all his troubles.

events.title: Heinrich Bullinger
events.note: Zwingli's successor as chief pastor of Zurich, who guided the Swiss Reformed church for over forty years and wrote the Second Helvetic Confession.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: He was born July 18, 1504, at Bremgarten in Aargau, the youngest of five sons of Dean Bullinger

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: A few weeks afterwards he died, after reciting several Psalms (51, 16, and 42), the Lord’s Prayer, and other prayers, peacefully, in the presence of his family, Sept. 17, 1575.

events.title: John Knox
events.note: Leader of the Scottish Reformation. A former priest who became a Protestant in 1545, he preached to English exiles at Geneva before returning to Scotland.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: John Knox (1505–1572), the Luther of Scotland, was educated in the University of Glasgow, and ordained to the Romish priesthood (1530)

second_source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
second_source.quote: He died, weary of life and longing for heaven, in the sixty-seventh year of his age, in peace, without a struggle, lamented by the clergy, the nobles, and the people (Nov. 24, 1572).

events.title: Reuchlin publishes his Hebrew grammar
events.note: Johann Reuchlin's De rudimentis hebraicis, a Hebrew grammar and dictionary, gave Christians in northern Europe a scientific basis for the study of Hebrew.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: He gave a scientific basis for the study of this language in his Hebrew Grammar and Dictionary, the De rudimentis hebraicis, which he published in 1506 at his own cost at Pforzheim.

events.title: John Calvin
events.note: French Reformer and theologian, born at Noyon in Picardy, who led the church at Geneva from 1541 until his death.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: John Calvin was born July 10, 1509,—twenty-five years after Luther and Zwingli,—at Noyon

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.locator: § 96. The First Years after the Return.
second_source.quote: Calvin entered at once upon his labors, and continued them without interruption for twenty-three years—till his death, May 27, 1564.

events.title: Fifth Lateran Council
events.note: The last general council of the Middle Ages, opened under Julius II and closed under Leo X. In 1516 it reaffirmed Unam Sanctam and rejected the supremacy of councils over the pope.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: At the 1st session, held May 3, 1512, there were present 16 cardinals, 12 patriarchs, 10 archbishops, 70 bishops and 3 generals of orders.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: The council adjourned March 16, 1517, a bare majority of two votes being for adjournment.

events.title: The Complutensian Polyglot printed
events.note: Cardinal Ximenes's polyglot Bible was printed in Spain. Its New Testament was printed in 1514 but not released to the public until 1520.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 77. The Study and Circulation of the Bible.
source.quote: Spain produced two editions, a Limousin version at Valencia,1478, and the Complutensian Bible of Cardinal Ximenes,1514–1517.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: It was hurried through the press in order to anticipate the publication of the New Testament of the Complutensian Polyglot, which was actually printed in 1514, but was not given to the public till 1520.

events.title: Erasmus publishes the Greek New Testament
events.note: Printed at Basel with the Greek text beside Erasmus's own Latin version and notes. His fourth and fifth editions became the basis of the textus receptus.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The appearance of Erasmus’ edition of the Greek Testament at Basel, 1516, marked an epoch in the study and understanding of the Scriptures.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: In all, Erasmus published five editions of the Greek Testament-1516, 1519, 1522, 1527 and 1535.

events.title: Luther publishes the German Theology
events.note: Luther issued a partial text of this anonymous devotional treatise by a Frankfurt priest in 1516 and a fuller edition in 1518. He said that next to the Bible and Augustine no book had taught him more.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The Reformer issued two editions of it, 1516, with a partial text, and 1518, in the second edition giving it the name which remains with it to this day, Ein Deutsch Theologia — A German treatise of Theology.

events.title: Luther posts the Ninety-five Theses
events.note: Luther posted ninety-five Latin theses on indulgences at the castle church in Wittenberg and invited a public disputation; the day came to be kept as the birthday of the Reformation.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: on the memorable thirty-first day of October, 1517, which has ever since been celebrated in Protestant Germany as the birthday of the Reformation, at twelve o’clock he affixed (either himself or through another) to the doors of the castle-church at Wittenberg, ninety-five Latin Theses

events.resource: First Principles of the Reformation (Ninety-five Theses and Three Primary Works).epub

events.title: Theodore Beza
events.note: Calvin's colleague and successor at Geneva, first rector of the Geneva Academy, and counsellor of the French Reformed churches.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 167. Life of Beza to his Conversion.
source.quote: They had already two sons and four daughters, when on the 24th of June in that year, 1519, another son was born who was destined to render the name illustrious to the end of time. This son was christened Theodore.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: On Sunday, Oct. 13, 1605, he died.

events.title: Leipzig Disputation
events.note: Johann Eck debated Carlstadt and then Luther in the Pleissenburg castle at Leipzig on free will, the papacy, purgatory and indulgences.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: § 37. The Leipzig Disputation. June 27-July 15, 1519.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: The second and more important act began July 4, between Eck and Luther, chiefly on the subject of the papacy.

events.title: Luther burns the pope's bull
events.note: Outside the Elster Gate at Wittenberg, before professors and students, Luther burned the papal bull that condemned his writings, together with the canon law. Schaff treats it as his final break with Rome.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 48. Luther burns the Pope’s bull, and forever breaks with Rome. Dec. 10, 1520.
source.quote: On the tenth day of December, 1520, at nine o’clock in the morning, in the presence of a large number of professors and students, he solemnly committed the bull of excommunication, together with the papal decretals, the Canon law, and several writings of Eck and Emser, to the flames

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: But he laughed it to scorn, and burned in revenge the pope’s bull, with all his decretals, Dec. 10, 1520.

events.title: Luther's tract on Christian Freedom
events.note: Sent to Pope Leo X with a dedicatory letter, the tract teaches that the Christian is lord of all by faith and servant of all by love.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 46. Christian Freedom.—Luther’s Last Letter to the Pope. October, 1520.
source.quote: Von der Freiheit eines Christenmenschen, Wittenberg, 1520; often reprinted separately, and in the collected works of Luther.

events.title: Luther before the Diet of Worms
events.note: Before Emperor Charles V, Luther refused to recant his books unless refuted by Scripture or clear reason. The Edict of Worms then put him under the ban of the empire.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 55. Luther’s Testimony before the Diet. April 17 and 18, 1521.
source.quote: On Thursday, the 18th of April, Luther appeared a second and last time before the Diet.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: On the 28th of January, 1521, Charles V. opened his first Diet at Worms.

events.title: Luther's German Bible
events.note: Luther translated the New Testament at the Wartburg; it appeared in September 1522, and the whole Bible, with the Apocrypha, was completed in 1534.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The translation was then hurried through three presses, and appeared already Sept. 21, 1522, but without his name.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: At last the whole Bible, including the Apocrypha as "books not equal to the Holy Scriptures, yet useful and good to read," was completed in 1534, and printed with numerous woodcuts.

events.title: First Zurich Disputation
events.note: A public disputation in German before about six hundred people in the Zurich city hall. The magistracy decided for Zwingli and directed him to keep preaching from the Scriptures.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The first disputation was held in the city hall on Thursday, Jan. 29, 1523, in the German language, before about six hundred persons, including all the clergy and members of the small and large Councils of Zurich.

events.title: Peasants' War
events.note: A rising of German peasants that began in Swabia and spread over south-western and central Germany. The princes crushed it in 1525, most decisively at Frankenhausen.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The insurrection broke out in summer, 1524, in Swabia, on the Upper Danube, and the Upper Rhine along the Swiss frontier, but not on the Swiss side, where the peasantry were free. In 1525 it extended gradually all over South-Western and Central Germany.

events.title: Grebel baptizes Blaurock: the Swiss Anabaptists begin
events.note: Soon after the Zurich disputation with Zwingli on infant baptism, Conrad Grebel baptized George Blaurock on his confession of faith at a private meeting, and Blaurock then baptized the others present. Schaff calls it the first case of rebaptism, a name the Anabaptists themselves rejected.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The first case was the rebaptism of Blaurock by Grebel in February, 1525, soon after the disputation with Zwingli.

events.title: Luther's Bondage of the Will
events.note: Luther's answer to Erasmus's treatise on the freedom of the will (1524), denying that the fallen human will is free in the things of salvation.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: He waited a whole year before he published his reply on the "Slavery of the Will" (December, 1525).

events.title: Tyndale's New Testament reaches England
events.note: The first New Testament translated into English from the Greek, printed on the Continent and brought into England, where church authorities burned copies.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.locator: Bible Versions, IV. English Versions, 3. Tyndale
source.quote: Both editions were in England by about March, 1526

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.locator: Bible Versions, IV. English Versions, 3. Tyndale
second_source.quote: The first public burning of the volume appears to have taken place in the autumn of 1526.

events.title: Luther's Large Catechism
events.note: Written after the Saxon church visitation, the Large Catechism is a continuous exposition of the Ten Commandments, the Creed, the Lord's Prayer and the sacraments, not divided into questions and answers. Luther wrote it before the Small Catechism of the same year.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: After several preparatory attempts, Luther wrote two Catechisms, in 1529, both in the German language—first the larger, and then the smaller.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: but after the doleful experience of popular ignorance during the church visitation, he took the task in hand himself, and completed it in 1529.

events.title: Luther's Small Catechism
events.note: Written after the Saxon church visitation showed how little the people knew, it explains the Ten Commandments, the Creed, the Lord's Prayer, Baptism and the Lord's Supper for households and children.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: Hence he prepared soon afterwards (in July, 1529) a short or little Catechism under the name Enchiridion.

second_source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
second_source.quote: After several preparatory attempts, Luther wrote two Catechisms, in 1529, both in the German language—first the larger, and then the smaller.

events.title: Marburg Colloquy
events.note: Philip of Hesse brought Luther and Melanchthon together with Zwingli and Oecolampadius at Marburg castle; they could not agree on Christ's presence in the Lord's Supper.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 107. The Marburg Conference, a.d. 1529. (With Facsimile of Signatures.)
source.quote: the famous Conference was held on the first three days of October. It was the first council among Protestants, and the first attempt to unite them.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: the fifteen Articles of Marburg, Oct. 4, 1529

events.title: Protest at the Diet of Speyer
events.note: The Lutheran princes and cities formally protested against the Diet's ban on further reform and appealed to a council; from this protest they were called Protestants.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 115. The Second Diet of Speier, and the Protest of 1529.
source.quote: the famous protest of April 25, 1529, against all those measures of the Diet which were contrary to the Word of God, to their conscience, and to the decision of the Diet of 1526

events.title: Augsburg Confession
events.note: Composed by Melanchthon and read in German before Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Augsburg; it became the chief confession of the Lutheran churches.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: On the 25th of June, 1530, the Confession was read aloud, in the German language, before the assembled representatives of Church and State, and in the hearing of a monarch in whose dominions the sun never set.

events.title: Apology of the Augsburg Confession
events.note: Melanchthon's defence of the Augsburg Confession against the Roman Catholic Confutation. The Diet refused his first draft in September 1530; the rewritten Apology was completed at Wittenberg.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.locator: § 42. The Apology of the Augsburg Confession, A.D. 1530–1531.
source.quote: On the following day Melanchthon left Augsburg in company with the Elector of Saxony, and re-wrote the Apology on the journey, and completed it at Wittenberg in April, 1531.

events.title: Battle of Kappel
events.note: The army of the Roman Catholic Forest Cantons routed the forces of Zurich at Kappel. Zwingli, who had gone with the Zurich troops, was killed.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The battle raged several hours in the afternoon of the eleventh of October, and was conducted by weapons and stones, after the manner of the Swiss, and with much bravery on both sides.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: the Waldstätters promptly organized an army of eight thousand men, and marched to the frontier of Zürich between Zug and Cappel, Oct. 9, 1531.

events.title: English Act of Supremacy
events.note: Parliament declared Henry VIII the only supreme head on earth of the Church of England, completing the break with papal jurisdiction.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: The rupture with Rome, at first attempted by means of gradual steps, was definitely accomplished in Nov., 1534, by the passing of the Act of Supremacy (26 Henry VIII., chap. 1), which conferred on the king the headship of the Church of England.

events.title: Calvin arrives in Geneva
events.note: Calvin meant to stay one night, but William Farel held him in Geneva by threatening him with the curse of God if he refused; he began lecturing on the epistles of Paul in September. The city expelled him and Farel in 1538.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 81. Calvin’s Arrival and Settlement at Geneva.
source.quote: Calvin arrived at Geneva in the later part of July, 1536, two months after the Reformation had been publicly introduced (May 21).

events.title: Calvin's Institutes of the Christian Religion
events.note: Calvin's systematic exposition of the Christian faith, first published at Basel with a preface to King Francis I of France. His last, much enlarged Latin edition appeared at Geneva in 1559.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 79. Calvin’s Institutes of the Christian Religion.
source.quote: The dedicatory Preface is dated ’X. Calendas Septembres’ (i.e. August 23), without the year; but at the close of the book the month of March, 1536, is given as the date of publication.

events.title: Smalcald Articles
events.note: Articles of faith drawn up by Luther for a proposed general council and signed by the Lutheran theologians at Smalcald; Melanchthon added an appendix on the power of the pope.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: Luther, by order of the Elector of Saxony (Dec. 11, 1536), prepared a Creed as a basis of negotiations at the Council, submitted it to Amsdorf, Agricola, Spalatin, and Melanchthon for approval, and sent it to the Elector, Jan. 3, 1537.

events.title: Calvin returns to Geneva
events.note: Expelled in 1538, Calvin was recalled from Strassburg and at once asked for a written church order. The Ecclesiastical Ordinances were ratified by the citizens on 2 January 1542.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: We have seen that in his first interview with the Syndics and Council after his return, Sept. 13, 1541, he insisted on the introduction of an ecclesiastical constitution and discipline in accordance with the Word of God and the primitive Church.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: He was expected at Geneva on the 9th of September, but did not arrive, it seems, before the 13th.

events.title: Council of Trent
events.note: Opened under Pope Paul III, the council met with long interruptions until 1563 and defined Roman Catholic doctrine in answer to the Reformation.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.locator: § 24. The Canons and Decrees of the Council of Trent.
source.quote: After long delays the Council was opened by order of Pope Paul III., in the Austrian City of Trent (since 1917, belonging to Italy), on the 13th December, 1545, and lasted, with long interruptions, till the 4th of December, 1563.

events.title: First Book of Common Prayer
events.note: The first English Prayer Book of Edward VI, chiefly the work of Archbishop Cranmer; a revised Second Prayer Book followed in 1552.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: The First Prayer-Book of Edward VI. was prepared and set forth (1549), and a few years afterwards the Second, with sundry changes (1552).

events.title: Consensus of Zurich
events.note: Calvin and Farel met Bullinger at Zurich and agreed twenty-six articles on the sacraments, uniting the Zurich and Geneva churches on the Lord's Supper. It was published in 1551.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: In May, 1549, he had, in company with Farel, a personal interview with Bullinger in Zurich at his cordial invitation, and drew up the Consensus as it now stands, in Twenty-six Articles. It was published in 1551 at Zurich and at Geneva.

events.title: Execution of Michael Servetus
events.note: The Spanish physician and anti-Trinitarian writer Michael Servetus, condemned for heresy by the Council of Geneva, was burned at Champel.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: At eleven o’clock on the 27th of October, Servetus was led from the prison to the gates of the City Hall, to hear the sentence read from the balcony by the Lord Syndic Darlod.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: He followed Servetus to the stake (Oct. 27, 1553), and exhorted him in vain to renounce his errors.

events.title: Marian persecution in England
events.note: Under Queen Mary, who restored the Roman obedience, Protestants were burned as heretics, among them the Reformers Cranmer, Latimer and Ridley at Oxford and the preacher John Bradford at Smithfield.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 12. Religious Intolerance and Liberty in England and America.
source.quote: 3. The reign of the bloody Queen Mary (1553–1558) was a fearful retaliation, but sealed the doom of popery by the blood of Protestant martyrs, including the Reformers, Cranmer, Latimer, and Ridley, who were burnt in the market place at Oxford.

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.quote: BRADFORD, JOHN: Church of England Protestant martyr; b. at Manchester about 1510; burned at Smithfield July 1, 1555.

events.title: Peace of Augsburg
events.note: A settlement at the Diet of Augsburg that gave the adherents of the Augsburg Confession legal standing in the Empire and left each secular ruler to determine the religion of his subjects.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: AUGSBURG, RELIGIOUS PEACE OF: A convention concluded in a diet at Augsburg Sept. 25, 1555, intended to settle the religious question in Germany.

second_source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
second_source.quote: The final result of the defeat of the Emperor was the Augsburg Treaty of Peace, 1555, which for the first time gave to the Lutherans a legal status in the empire, though with certain restrictions.

events.title: Genevan missionaries reach Brazil
events.note: Pierre Richer and Guillaume Chartier, the first Protestant missionaries in America, came from Geneva with Reformed colonists to Villegagnon's French colony at Rio de Janeiro. Disputes soon broke up the mission.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: In Nov., 1556, they embarked at Honfleur, under the command of Villegagnon’s nephew, Bois le Conte, and in Mar., 1557, the three ships arrived, with nearly 300 colonists.

events.title: Gallican Confession
events.note: The first national synod of the Reformed churches of France, meeting in Paris, adopted a confession of faith drafted by Calvin and enlarged by Antoine de la Roche Chandieu, together with a Presbyterian church order.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: The first national Synod was held in Paris, May 25–28, 1559, under the moderatorship of François de Morel, then pastor of Paris, a friend and pupil of Calvin. It gave the Reformed Church a compact organization by the adoption of the Gallican Confession of Faith

events.title: Academy of Geneva dedicated
events.note: Calvin's academy for the education of ministers and scholars was dedicated in the church of St. Peter, and Theodore Beza was proclaimed its first rector.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 161. The Academy of Geneva. The High School of Reformed Theology.
source.quote: The Academy was solemnly dedicated on June 5, 1559, in the church of St. Peter, in the presence of the whole Council, the ministers, and six hundred students.

events.title: Geneva Bible
events.note: English Bible finished at Geneva by the Protestant exiles William Whittingham, Anthony Gilby and Thomas Sampson. It became the Bible most used in English homes.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.locator: Bible Versions, IV. English Versions, 4. Coverdale. Other Editions
source.quote: In 1558 Coverdale began in Geneva a new Bible, but returned to England in 1559, while Whittingham, Anthony Gilby, and Thomas Sampson finished the printing of the handsome edition known as the "Geneva" Bible in Apr., 1560.

events.title: Scots Confession
events.note: Drawn up in four days by John Knox and his colleagues at the direction of the Scottish Parliament, which ratified it; acts abolishing the mass and papal jurisdiction followed.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.locator: § 89. The Scotch Confession of Faith. A.D. 1560.
source.quote: The document was read twice, article by article, and ratified by the three estates, August 17, 1560, 'as a doctrine grounded upon the infallible Word of God.'

events.title: Belgic Confession
events.note: Written in French by Guido de Brès to set out the Reformed faith of the Low Countries. It was later revised and adopted by the Synod of Dort.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: The Belgic Confession was prepared in 1561 by Guido de Brès, with the aid of Adrien de Saravia (professor of theology in Leyden, afterwards at Cambridge, where he died, 1613), H. Modetus (for some time chaplain of William of Orange), and G. Wingen, in the French language

events.title: Heidelberg Catechism
events.note: Prepared at the order of Elector Frederick of the Palatinate and published with his preface dated 19 January 1563. It became one of the most widely used Reformed catechisms.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: It was published early in 1563, in German, under the title 'Catechismus, Or Christian Instruction, as conducted in the Churches and Schools of the Electoral Palatinate.' It is preceded by a short Preface of the Elector, dated Tuesday, January 19, 1563

events.title: Thirty-nine Articles
events.note: The Church of England's articles of religion, revised from the Forty-two Articles of 1553 and ratified by Convocation in 1563; the authorized English text followed in 1571.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: After an examination by both houses, the Articles, reduced to the number of thirty-nine, were ratified and signed by the Bishops and the members of the lower house, and published by the royal press, 1563.

second_source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
second_source.quote: The authorized English text was adopted by Convocation in 1571, and issued under the editorial care of Bishop Jewel of Salesbury.

events.title: Second Helvetic Confession
events.note: Written by Heinrich Bullinger as his personal confession and published at Zurich in Latin and German. It became the most widely adopted Reformed confession on the Continent after the Heidelberg Catechism.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The new Confession was published at Zürich, March 12, 1566, in both languages, at public expense, and was forwarded to the Elector of the Palatinate and to Philip of Hesse.

events.title: St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre
events.note: Very many Huguenots were murdered in Paris on St. Bartholomew's Day, and the killings were repeated in other parts of France for days afterwards.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.locator: § 172. Beza as the Successor of Calvin, down to 1586.
source.quote: On St. Bartholomew’s Day, Sunday, Aug. 24, 1572, very many Protestants were murdered in Paris, and for days thereafter the shocking scenes were repeated in different parts of France.

events.title: Book of Concord
events.note: The collected Lutheran confessions, including the Formula of Concord of 1577, published at Dresden on the fiftieth anniversary of the Augsburg Confession.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: Three years elapsed before the new symbolical book was signed and solemnly published, by order of Augustus, at Dresden, June 25, 1580, the fiftieth anniversary of the Augsburg Confession, together with the other Lutheran symbols, in one volume, called the 'Book of Concord,'

events.title: Edict of Nantes
events.note: Issued by Henry IV of France, it gave the Huguenots a limited legal toleration, placing them on a nearly common footing with Roman Catholics.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: when in 1598, he published the Edict of Nantes, which put the Protestants on a nearly common footing with the Roman Catholics in France

events.title: The Arminian Remonstrance
events.note: Followers of Jacobus Arminius set out five articles on predestination, the extent of the atonement, faith, the resistibility of grace and perseverance, and laid them before the States of Holland. The Synod of Dort answered them.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: The peculiar tenets are contained in the five points or articles which the Arminians in their 'Remonstrance' laid before the estates of Holland in 1610.

events.title: King James Version
events.note: Proposed by John Reynolds at the Hampton Court Conference in 1604 and made by six companies of scholars appointed by James I; it became known as the Authorized Version.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.locator: Bible Versions, IV. English Versions, 6. The Authorized Version
source.quote: After years of labor (although some say that the work really began only in 1607 and lasted but two years and a half), during which some passages were wrought over fourteen or even seventeen times, the version appeared in 1611 in two folio editions

events.title: Richard Baxter
events.note: Puritan pastor at Kidderminster and author of The Saints' Everlasting Rest and The Reformed Pastor. After 1662 he preached as a Nonconformist and was imprisoned from 1685 to 1686.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: b. at Rowton (42 m. n.e. of Shrewsbury), Shropshire, Nov. 12, 1615; d. in London Dec. 8, 1691.

events.title: John Owen
events.note: Independent (Congregational) theologian, dean of Christ Church and vice-chancellor of Oxford during the Commonwealth. He wrote the preface to the Savoy Declaration of 1658.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: Independent scholar and Reformer; b. at Stadham or Stadhampton (5 m. s.s.e. of Oxford) in 1616; d. at Ealing (9 m. w. of St. Paul's Cathedral, London) Aug. 24, 1683.

events.title: Synod of Dort
events.note: National synod of the Dutch Reformed Church, with delegates from other Reformed churches, which judged the Arminian Remonstrance and adopted the Canons of Dort on its five points.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: At last, after a great deal of controversy and complicated preparations, the National Synod of Dort was convened by the States-General, Nov. 13, 1618, and lasted till May 9, 1619.

events.title: Thirty Years' War
events.note: A religious and political war between Protestant and Roman Catholic powers, fought chiefly in Germany. It began in Bohemia and ended with the Peace of Westphalia.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: The great religious struggle of the seventeenth century (1618–1648) between the Protestants and the Roman Catholics, Germany being the chief area of conflict.

events.title: Pilgrim Fathers sail for America
events.note: English Separatists who had lived in Leyden since 1609 crossed to New England on the Mayflower and founded the colony of Plymouth.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.locator: The Arminian Controversy and the Synod of Dort, A.D. 1604–1619, note
source.quote: In the same year (1609) the Pilgrim Fathers of New England arrived in Leyden, where they enjoyed religions freedom till their departure for America (1620).

events.title: John Bunyan
events.note: Baptist preacher of Bedford, imprisoned in the county jail there from 1660 to 1672 for his preaching, and author of The Pilgrim's Progress and Grace Abounding. The source gives his christening, Nov. 30, 1628, rather than his birth date.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: b. at Harrowden (1 m. s.e. of Bedford), in the parish of Elstow, christened Nov. 30, 1628; d. in London Aug. 31, 1688.

events.title: Scottish National Covenant signed
events.note: At Greyfriars' Church, Edinburgh, Scots renewed the Covenant of 1581 with a protest against the government of the Kirk by bishops and against the religious measures of Charles I. Schaff says it marks the Second Reformation.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.locator: § 90. The Scotch Covenants and the Scotch Kirk.
source.quote: The renewal of the Covenant took place in Greyfriars' Church, in Edinburgh, the 28th of February, 1638, and was a most solemn and extraordinary scene.

events.title: Solemn League and Covenant
events.note: A covenant between Scotland and the English Parliament for the reformation and defence of religion, drafted by Alexander Henderson; the Commons and the Westminster Assembly swore it on 25 September 1643.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.locator: § 90. The Scotch Covenants and the Scotch Kirk.
source.quote: The draft was unanimously and enthusiastically adopted by the General Assembly and the Scottish Convention, Aug. 17, 1643.

events.title: Westminster Assembly
events.note: An assembly of divines called by the English Parliament, joined by Scottish commissioners, to reform the Church of England. It produced the Westminster Confession and Catechisms.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: The Assembly occupied about five years and six months for the completion of its proper work—the standards of doctrine, worship, and discipline—and held no less than 1163 regular sessions from July 1, 1643, till February 22, 1649

events.title: John Eliot begins preaching to Native Americans
events.note: After two years of studying their language, John Eliot, Puritan minister of Roxbury in Massachusetts, preached his first sermon to an assembly of Indians at Nonantum. He later translated the whole Bible into their language.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: Having prepared himself by two years’ study of their language, he preached for the first time to an assembly of Indians at Nonantum, in the present town of Newton, Oct. 28, 1646.

events.title: Westminster Confession of Faith
events.note: Completed by the Westminster Assembly and presented to both Houses of Parliament; the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland adopted it on 27 August 1647.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: In the 752d Session, Dec. 4, 1646, the Confession was completed and presented to both Houses of Parliament in a copy transcribed with great pains by Dr. Burgess

second_source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
second_source.quote: The General Assembly at Edinburgh, Aug. 27, 1647, after careful examination, adopted it in full as it came from the hands of the Westminster divines

events.title: Westminster Larger Catechism
events.note: Chiefly the work of Anthony Tuckney, it was presented to Parliament in the autumn of 1647 and adopted by the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland on 20 July 1648.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: The Catechisms were finished and presented to Parliament for examination and approval in the autumn of 1647.

second_source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
second_source.quote: The General Assembly at Edinburgh adopted the Larger Catechism, July 20, 1648, and the Shorter Catechism, July 28

events.title: Westminster Shorter Catechism
events.note: Prepared after the Larger Catechism and presented to Parliament in the autumn of 1647; the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland adopted it on 28 July 1648.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: The Catechisms were finished and presented to Parliament for examination and approval in the autumn of 1647.

second_source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
second_source.quote: The General Assembly at Edinburgh adopted the Larger Catechism, July 20, 1648, and the Shorter Catechism, July 28

events.title: Peace of Westphalia
events.note: The treaties that ended the Thirty Years' War and secured legal standing for both the Lutheran and the Reformed confessions in Germany.

source.work: Schaff, History of the Christian Church
source.quote: The Reformation period begins with Luther’s Theses, a.d. 1517, and ends with the Peace of Westphalia, a.d. 1648. The last event brought to a close the terrible Thirty Years’ War and secured a legal existence to the Protestant faith (the Lutheran and Reformed Confession) throughout Germany.

events.title: Synod of Cambridge adopts the Westminster Confession
events.note: A synod of New England Congregational churches consented to the Westminster Confession "for the substance thereof" and agreed a Platform of Church Discipline, known as the Cambridge Platform.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: The 'Elders and Messengers of the churches assembled in the Synod at Cambridge, in New England,' in June, 1648, adopted the Westminster Confession one year after its publication

events.title: Baxter's The Reformed Pastor
events.note: Baxter's treatise on the work of the pastor, written during his ministry at Kidderminster.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: The after-world knows him by reputation as the author of The Reformed Pastor (1656), a treatise on pastoral theology still usable;

events.title: Savoy Declaration
events.note: About two hundred delegates of English Congregational churches, meeting at the Savoy in London from Sept. 29 to Oct. 12, 1658, agreed on a declaration of faith and order based on the Westminster Confession, changed chiefly on church government.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: About two hundred delegates from one hundred and twenty congregations attended the Conference, which lasted from Sept. 29 till Oct. 12, 1658. They agreed unanimously upon the Confession and Order of Discipline.

events.title: The Great Ejection
events.note: The Act of Uniformity took effect on St. Bartholomew's Day, requiring conformity to the revised Prayer Book and episcopal ordination; more than two thousand Puritan ministers who would not conform lost their livings.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: The Act of Uniformity, which received the royal assent May 19, 1662, and took effect on the ominous St. Bartholomew's Day, Aug. 24, 1662

second_source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
second_source.quote: By this cruel act more than two thousand Puritan rectors and vicars—that is, about one fifth of the English clergy, including such men as Baxter, Howe, Poole, Owen, Goodwin, Bates, Manton, Caryl—were ejected

events.title: Isaac Watts
events.note: Nonconformist pastor in London called the founder of English hymnody; his Hymns (1707) and Psalms of David (1719) had tremendous success and made hymn-singing an earnest devotional power.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: WATTS, ISAAC: Founder of English hymnody; b. at Southampton, England, July 17, 1674; d. at Stoke Newington (4 m. n.e. of Charing Cross, London) Nov. 25, 1748.

events.title: Helvetic Consensus Formula
events.note: Drawn up by John Henry Heidegger of Zurich with Francis Turretin and Lucas Gernler to defend the teaching of the Synod of Dort against the theology of Saumur. It was the last doctrinal confession of the Reformed Church of Switzerland.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: It was composed in 1675, one hundred and eleven years after Calvin's death, by Professor John Henry Heidegger, of Zurich (1633–1698), at the request and with the co-operation of the Rev. Lucas Gernler, of Basle (d. 1675), and Professor Francis Turretin, of Geneva (1623–1687).

events.title: Spener publishes Pia Desideria
events.note: Philipp Jakob Spener's short book urged wider Bible study, the spiritual priesthood of all believers and practical piety, and became a founding text of German Pietism.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.locator: Pietism, I. Philipp Jakob Spener, § 3. The Pia Desideria
source.quote: The event that formed an epoch in Spener's life and attracted wide attention was the publication of his little Pia desideria (Frankfort, 1675).

events.title: Second London Baptist Confession
events.note: The Particular (Calvinistic) Baptists' confession, containing the body of the Westminster Confession, appeared in London in 1677 and was approved by messengers of over a hundred congregations in 1689. The Philadelphia Baptist Association adopted it in 1742.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: It appeared first in 1677, at London, under the title, 'A Confession of Faith put forth by the Elders and Brethren of many congregations of Christians baptized upon profession of their faith.'

second_source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
second_source.quote: It was reprinted in 1688, 1689, and approved and recommended by the ministers and messengers of above a hundred congregations met in London, July 3–11, 1689.

events.title: Bunyan publishes The Pilgrim's Progress
events.note: The first part of Bunyan's allegory appeared in London in 1678, having been begun during his imprisonment; the second part followed in 1684.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: All the world knows that Bunyan wrote The Pilgrim's Progress, in two parts, of which the first appeared at London in 1678, and was at all events, begun during his imprisonment in 1676; the second in 1684.

events.title: Revocation of the Edict of Nantes
events.note: Louis XIV revoked the edict of 1598 that had given French Protestants a limited toleration, and a great exodus of Huguenots followed.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: The further development of the Saumur theology was arrested by the political oppression which culminated in the cruel revocation of the Edict of Nantes by Louis XIV. (1685)

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.quote: issued by Henry IV. in 1598 and revoked by Louis XIV. in 1685.

events.title: Toleration Act
events.note: Passed under William and Mary for the relief of Dissenters, it gave Nonconformist churches such as the Baptists partial legal protection and exempted dissenting ministers from subscribing some of the Thirty-nine Articles.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.locator: § 97. Criticism of the Westminster System of Doctrine.
source.quote: The Toleration Act of May 24, 1689, for the relief of Dissenters, marks the transition.

second_source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
second_source.quote: The Act of Toleration (1689) brought relief to the Baptists, and enabled them to build chapels and spread throughout the country.

events.title: John Wesley
events.note: Anglican clergyman and father of Methodism; the Oxford "holy club" of 1729 marks the movement's beginning, and he spent more than fifty years in field-preaching.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: John Wesley, the father of the doctrinal and practical system of Methodism, was born at Epworth (23 m. n.w. of Lincoln) June 28, 1703, and died in London Mar. 2, 1791.

events.title: Jonathan Edwards
events.note: Congregational pastor at Northampton, Massachusetts, from 1727 to 1750 and a leading theologian of the Great Awakening. He died five weeks after being inaugurated president of the college at Princeton.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: b. at Windsor Farms (now East Windsor), Conn., Oct. 5, 1703; d. at Princeton, N. J., Mar. 22, 1758.

events.title: Ziegenbalg begins the Tranquebar mission
events.note: Bartholomaeus Ziegenbalg, trained at Halle and sent by the king of Denmark, became the first German Protestant missionary to India; he learned Tamil and translated the New Testament into it.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: Landing in Tranquebar in July, 1706, Ziegenbalg and his companion began their labors under the most adverse conditions

events.title: George Whitefield
events.note: Calvinistic Methodist evangelist who began open-air preaching near Bristol in 1739 and made seven visits to America, where his tours spread the revival among Congregationalists, Presbyterians and Baptists.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: WHITEFIELD, GEORGE: Calvinistic Methodist; b. in Gloucester, England, Dec. 27, 1714; d. in Newburyport, Mass., Sept. 30, 1770.

events.title: David Brainerd
events.note: Missionary to the American Indians in New York, Pennsylvania and New Jersey, with his greatest success at Crossweeksung. He died of consumption at Jonathan Edwards's home in Northampton, and Edwards edited his papers.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: BRAINERD, DAVID: Missionary to the American Indians; b. at Haddam, Conn., Apr. 20, 1718; d. at the home of Jonathan Edwards (to whose daughter Jemima he was engaged), Northampton, Mass., Oct. 9, 1747.

events.title: Moravian refugees settle at Herrnhut
events.note: Refugees from Moravia led by Christian David settled on Count Zinzendorf's estate at Berthelsdorf in Saxony and built the town of Herrnhut, the centre of the renewed Moravian Church.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.locator: Unity of the Brethren (Unitas Fratrum), I. History, § 2. Beginnings at Herrnhut, p. 91
source.quote: In 1722 two families named Neisser, led by Christian David, "the servant of the Lord," fled from Moravia, and, by invitation of Count Zinzendorf (q.v.), settled on his domain of Berthelsdorf in Saxony.

second_source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
second_source.quote: The asylum was called Herrnhut (the Lord's Protection), and became the mother church and the centre of the denomination.

events.title: Adopting Act of the Synod of Philadelphia
events.note: The synod of American Presbyterians required its ministers to declare their agreement with the Westminster Confession and Catechisms and adopted the Confession as the confession of their faith.

source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
source.quote: The Synod of Philadelphia, Sept. 19, 1729, adopted the Confession with a liberal construction, in these words:

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.locator: Presbyterians, VIII. In the United States and Canada, 1. The Presbyterian Church in the United States of America, 3. Colonial Presbyterian Church
second_source.quote: The general synod in 1729 passed what is called the Adopting Act, by which it was agreed that all the ministers under its jurisdiction should declare "their agreement in and approbation of the Confession of Faith, with the Larger and Shorter Catechism of the assembly of divines at Westminster,"

events.title: Moravian missions begin on St. Thomas
events.note: Leonard Dober and David Nitschmann began the Moravian foreign missionary work on the island of St. Thomas; missions to Greenland, North America, Suriname and South Africa followed within a few years.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.locator: Unity of the Brethren (Unitas Fratrum), V. Enterprises of the Church, § 2. Missions, p. 93
source.quote: In 1732 Leonard Dober and David Nitschmann (q.v.) inaugurated on the island of St. Thomas that work

second_source.work: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom
second_source.quote: Their chief glory lies in the extraordinary zeal and self-denial with which, since 1732, they have labored

events.title: Northampton revival under Jonathan Edwards
events.note: A revival began in Edwards's congregation at Northampton, Massachusetts, after his sermons on justification by faith; about three hundred people were converted in half a year.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: In 1734–35 there occurred in his parish a "great awakening" of religious feeling

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.locator: Revivals of Religion, III. In America, 1. Revivals under Edwards, p. 11
second_source.quote: But the history of American revivals, as a distinct element of the religious life, begins properly in 1734 with the preaching of a series of sermons by Edwards, at Northampton, upon justification by faith.

events.title: The Great Awakening
events.note: A second and wider revival spread through much of New England, carried from place to place by George Whitefield's preaching tour, which reached Northampton in October 1740, and by preachers such as Gilbert Tennent.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: in 1740–41 occurred another, which extended through a large part of New England (see Revivals of Religion)

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.locator: Revivals of Religion, III. In America, 1. Revivals under Edwards, p. 11
second_source.quote: In the spring of 1740 the spirit of revival was again present.

events.title: Edwards's Religious Affections
events.note: Edwards's treatise on how to tell the religious affections that are signs of true grace from those that are not, written after the revivals of the Great Awakening.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: A Treatise concerning Religious Affections (1746), one of his most spiritual and analytical works;

events.title: Edwards's Freedom of the Will
events.note: Written after Edwards left his Northampton pastorate, the treatise argues against the notion of a self-determining will that Arminian writers held to be necessary to moral agency.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: some of them not until after his death, viz.: A Careful and Strict Enquiry into the Modern Prevailing Notions of that Freedom of Will which is Supposed to be Essential to Moral Agency (1754);

events.title: William Carey
