events.note: English Baptist shoemaker and preacher whose efforts founded the Baptist Missionary Society; he sailed for India in 1793. From Serampore he and his colleagues translated the Bible, in whole or in part, into some twenty-six Indian languages.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: b. at Paulerspury, Northamptonshire, Eng., Aug. 17, 1761; d. at Serampur, India, June 9, 1834.

events.title: Thomas Chalmers
events.note: Scottish minister whose preaching and parish work among the poor of Glasgow made him famous. In 1843 he led the ministers who left the established church and was the first moderator of the Free Church of Scotland.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: b. in East Anstruther, Fifeshire, Mar. 17, 1780; d. in Edinburgh May 30, 1847.

events.title: Baptist Missionary Society founded
events.note: After William Carey's sermon "Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God," Particular Baptists meeting at Kettering formed a missionary society; Carey sailed for India the next year.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: On Oct. 2, 1792, largely through his exertions, the first Baptist missionary society was founded

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.locator: Baptists, I. The English Baptists, 4. Particular Baptists from 1644 Onward, § 5. Andrew Fuller. Missionary Enterprise
second_source.quote: preached a sermon on the topic: “Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God,” which made a profound impression and led to the organization, a few months later (Oct. 2), at Kettering (Fuller’s church) of the Baptist Missionary Society.

events.title: London Missionary Society founded
events.note: A society for missions to the heathen was organized in London in 1795 with the support of several denominations; it came in time to be sustained mainly by Congregationalists.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.locator: Congregationalists, I. History, 1. The English Congregationalists, § 11 Missionary Work (p. 233)
source.quote: The London Missionary Society was organized in 1795. At first several denominations united in its support, but for some time it has been sustained mainly by Congregationalists.

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.quote: He was one of the founders of the London Missionary Society (1795), of the Religion Tract Society (1799), and of the British and Foreign Bible Society (1804)

events.title: Charles Hodge
events.note: American Presbyterian theologian who taught at Princeton Theological Seminary from 1822 until his death.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: American theologian; b. at Philadelphia Dec. 18, 1797; d. at Princeton, N. J., June 19, 1878.

events.title: Church Missionary Society founded
events.note: Evangelicals in the Church of England, among them John Venn, Charles Simeon and William Wilberforce, founded the Church Missionary Society for Africa and the East.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.locator: Missions to the Heathen, B. Protestant Missions, II. Colonial Missions, 3. The Present Mission Era, § 2 Carey and the English Missionary Societies (p. 408)
source.quote: such members of the Evangelical party in the Established Church as came together under the leadership of John Venn, Charles Simeon, William Wilberforce, and others, united for the founding of an Anglican missionary society, the Church Missionary Society for Africa and the East, in 1799.

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.quote: Sunday Schools were organized by the layman Robert Raikes of Gloucester in 1780, and in 1799 the Church Missionary Society was founded

events.title: British and Foreign Bible Society founded
events.note: The society grew out of a public meeting at the London Tavern, where churchmen and Dissenters joined to circulate the Bible without note or comment.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.locator: Bible Societies, I. British Bible Societies, 2. The British and Foreign Bible Society, 1. Origin and Constitution
source.quote: On Mar. 7, 1804, a public meeting was held at the London Tavern, on the call of Mr. Hughes. Three hundred persons attended the meeting. It was quickly evident that a society for increasing the circulation of the Bible presented common ground, upon which all sects and parties could stand.

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.quote: He was one of the founders of the London Missionary Society (1795), of the Religion Tract Society (1799), and of the British and Foreign Bible Society (1804)

events.title: Robert Morrison reaches Canton
events.note: Robert Morrison, sent by the London Missionary Society as the pioneer of Protestant missions in China, arrived at Canton; with William Milne he translated the whole Bible into Chinese, printed in 1819.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.locator: China, II. Christian Missions, 3. Protestant Missions, § 1 First Period, to 1842 (p. 33)
source.quote: In this vast field the London Missionary Society had the honor of being the pioneer, in the face of difficulties which can now be but imperfectly comprehended. Robert Morrison (q. v.) reached Canton by way of New York Sept. 7, 1807.

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.quote: was ordained Jan., 1807, and then sailed for Canton. He became interpreter for the East India Company

events.title: British slave trade declared illegal
events.note: After a long campaign led in Parliament by William Wilberforce, the slave trade was outlawed; slavery itself was abolished in the English colonies in 1834.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.locator: Missions to the Heathen, B. Protestant Missions, II. Colonial Missions, 3. The Present Mission Era, § 1 Events Leading to Renewed Effort (p. 407)
source.quote: The leader in this agitation was William Wilberforce (q.v.). After a struggle of nineteen years, the slave-trade was at last, in 1807, declared illegal, and in 1834 slavery itself was abolished in the English colonies.

events.title: American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions founded
events.note: Organized after Adoniram Judson and fellow young men Mills, Nott and Newell submitted a statement to the General Association of Ministers at Bradford, Massachusetts, the board became the agency of Congregational foreign missions.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.locator: Congregationalists, I. History, 4. Congregationalists in America, § 11 The American Board (p. 236)
source.quote: Congregational foreign mission work is in charge of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions. Established in 1810, it has had successful missions among the Choctaw and Cherokee Indians

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.quote: that illustrious band of young men—Mills, Nott, Newell, and Richards, and joined the first three in submitting a statement to the General Association of Ministers at Bradford, Mass., which led to the organization of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions.

events.title: Princeton Theological Seminary organized
events.note: The General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church entrusted Archibald Alexander with organizing its theological seminary at Princeton, New Jersey, where he was the first professor.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: In 1812 he was entrusted by the General Assembly with the organization of the Princeton Theological Seminary. For the first year he taught all departments

events.title: David Livingstone
events.note: Scottish missionary of the London Missionary Society and explorer of southern and central Africa.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: Explorer and missionary in Africa, was born at Blantyre (8 m. s.e. of Glasgow) Mar. 19, 1813, and died in Ilala, Central Africa, May 1, 1873.

events.title: Adoniram Judson lands at Rangoon
events.note: Kept from missionary work in India by the East India Company, the American missionary Adoniram Judson settled at Rangoon, Burma; the first Burmese convert was baptized there in 1819.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: The East India Company forbade his prosecution of missionary labors in India; and, after various vicissitudes, he landed in July, 1813, at Rangoon, Burma, taking up his residence at the Mission House of Felix Carey.

events.title: Charles Haddon Spurgeon
events.note: English Baptist preacher, pastor in London from 1854 until his death; he founded the Pastors' College and published a sermon every week.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: English Baptist; b. at Kelvedon (40 m. n.e. of London), Essex, June 19, 1834; d. at Mentone (13 m. n.e. of Nice), France, Jan. 31, 1892.

events.title: Secession from the Netherlands Reformed Church
events.note: After the Evangelical minister De Cock was deposed, a secession from the state Reformed Church in Holland was resolved upon; the seceders organized the Christian Reformed Church.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.locator: Holland, I. Protestant Churches, 2. The Christian Reformed Church (Christelijke Gereformeerde Kerken) (p. 320)
source.quote: With the deposition of one of the Evangelical ministers, De Cock, because he would not conform in certain matters, a crisis came in 1834, and the Evangelical party came into conflict with the authorities, and a secession was resolved upon.

events.title: Disruption of the Church of Scotland
events.note: In a dispute with the civil courts over the settling of ministers on unwilling congregations, 470 ministers left the General Assembly and formed the Free Church of Scotland under Thomas Chalmers.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.locator: Chalmers, Thomas; The Organization of the Free Church
source.quote: No help came; and accordingly, on May 18, 1843, four hundred and seventy clergymen withdrew from the General Assembly, and constituted themselves into the Free Church of Scotland, electing Dr. Chalmers as their first moderator.

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.locator: Presbyterians, I. Scotland, 3. Free Church of Scotland
second_source.quote: The Free Church of Scotland began its separate existence at the disruption of the Church of Scotland in 1843 (see above, 1, § 4), under the leadership of Dr. Thomas Chalmers.

events.title: Samuel Crowther consecrated bishop of the Niger
events.note: Samuel Adjai Crowther, a Yoruba freed from a slave ship and educated in the Church of England mission at Sierra Leone, was consecrated the first bishop of the Niger.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: In 1844 he began the Yoruba mission. On June 29th, 1864, he was consecrated first bishop of the Niger in Canterbury Cathedral.

events.title: China Inland Mission founded
events.note: J. Hudson Taylor founded a new society to evangelize inland China and sailed with a party of sixteen missionaries in May 1866.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: In 1865, at Brighton, Taylor definitely dedicated himself to God for the founding of a new society to undertake the evangelization of inland China.

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.locator: China, II. Christian Missions, 3. Protestant Missions, § 3 The Third Period, 1860–95 (p. 34)
second_source.quote: The most important single step in the evangelization of China was the development (rather than the organization) of the China Inland Mission (1865), founded on a combination of faith and works

events.title: First Vatican Council
events.note: Called by Pius IX and held in St. Peter's, Rome, the council defined papal infallibility at its fourth public session on 18 July 1870 and was prorogued in October 1870.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.locator: Vatican Council, II. Proceedings of the Council, 1. From the Opening, until Mar. 6, 1870, § 2 First and Second Sessions (p. 149)
source.quote: The first public session took place Wednesday Dec. 8, 1869, with the opening on a festival.

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.locator: Vatican Council, II. Proceedings of the Council, 3. Fourth Session, Monday July 18, 1870 (p. 152)
second_source.quote: 3. Fourth Session, Monday July 18, 1870: Worthy of note here are the attempts of some bishops of the minority to enlighten, along literary lines, their fellow synodical delegates

events.title: Spurgeon's The Treasury of David
events.note: Charles Spurgeon's exposition of the Psalms in seven volumes, drawing on the Puritan divines.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: His most important work was The Treasury of David, an exposition of the book of Psalms (7 vols., 1870–1885).

events.title: Hodge's Systematic Theology
events.note: Charles Hodge's principal work, a Systematic Theology in three volumes running to 2,260 pages.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: His magnum opus is the Systematic Theology (1871–1873), of 3 vols. 8vo. and extending to 2,260 pages.

events.title: Alliance of the Reformed Churches formed
events.note: Delegates of Presbyterian and Reformed churches met in London and prepared a constitution for an alliance of churches holding the Presbyterian system, popularly called the Presbyterian Alliance.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.locator: Alliance of the Reformed Churches; Origin
source.quote: The proposal met with such general approval that in July, 1875, a conference was held at the English Presbyterian College in London.

second_source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
second_source.locator: Alliance of the Reformed Churches; Origin
second_source.quote: A voluntary organization formed in London in 1875, on the model of the Evangelical Alliance; but confined to Churches of presbyterial polity and more churchly in the character of its representation.

events.title: Abraham Kuyper founds the Free University
events.note: Abraham Kuyper, a Dutch Calvinist theologian and later prime minister, founded the Free University at Amsterdam and taught there.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: In 1880 he founded at Amsterdam the Free University, where he has since been professor, lecturing on various topics as occasion requires.

events.title: Bavinck's Reformed Dogmatics
events.note: Herman Bavinck, then professor of dogmatic theology at the seminary in Kampen, published his Gereformeerde Dogmatiek in four volumes.

source.work: The New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge
source.quote: De algemeene Genade (1894); Gereformeerde Dogmatiek (4 vols., 1895–1901); Beginselen der Psychologie (1897)

events.title: Armenian genocide begins
events.note: During the First World War the Ottoman government began deporting and killing the empire's Armenian Christians. The U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum estimates that at least 664,000 and possibly as many as 1.2 million were killed.

source.work: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, Holocaust Encyclopedia
source.locator: The Armenian Genocide (1915-16): Overview, Key Facts
source.quote: The Armenian genocide took place between the spring of 1915 and the fall of 1916. At least 664,000 and possibly as many as 1.2 million Armenians were killed.

second_source.work: Armenian Genocide Museum-Institute (Yerevan)
second_source.locator: Armenian Genocide: What is the Armenian Genocide?
second_source.quote: The extermination of Armenians in the Ottoman Empire and the surrounding regions during 1915-1923 is called the Armenian Genocide.

events.title: Westminster Theological Seminary opens
events.note: J. Gresham Machen, who had resigned from Princeton Theological Seminary, founded Westminster Theological Seminary in Philadelphia. It opened with fifty students.

source.work: The Orthodox Presbyterian Church, Today in OPC History
source.quote: On September 25, 1929, Westminster Theological Seminary opened in the Witherspoon building in Philadelphia, with an enrollment of fifty students.

second_source.work: PCA Historical Center, This Day in Presbyterian History
second_source.quote: The happy fruition of this meeting on that same year of 1929 was September 25, in which fifty students gathered at the Seminary campus at 1528 Pine Street in Philadelphia.

events.title: Barmen Theological Declaration
events.note: The Confessional Synod at Barmen, uniting Lutheran, Reformed and United churches, adopted six theses rejecting the teaching of the "German Christians", a movement that aligned the church with National Socialism. It became the central theological statement of the Confessing Church.

source.work: Evangelical Church in Germany (EKD)
source.quote: The Theological Declaration from the Synod in Barmen from May 31st, 1934, is the central thological statement of the Confessing Church under the regime of the National Socialists 1933-1945.

second_source.work: Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.), The Book of Confessions (2016)
second_source.quote: The Confessional Synod of the German Evangelical Church met in Barmen, May 29–31, 1934.

events.title: Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran
events.note: Bedouin shepherds found jars of ancient scrolls in a cave near the Dead Sea. The seven scrolls of this first find began a search of the Qumran caves that lasted nearly a decade.

source.work: Israel Antiquities Authority, The Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library
source.locator: Learn about the Scrolls: Discovery Sites
source.quote: Qumran Cave 1 (1Q) – Discovered by a young Bedouin shepherd in 1947 and excavated by archaeologists in 1949. The first Dead Sea Scrolls were found in this cave, later called Cave 1.

second_source.work: Library of Congress, Scrolls from the Dead Sea (exhibition)
second_source.quote: In 1947, young Bedouin shepherds, searching for a stray goat in the Judean Desert, entered a long-untouched cave and found jars filled with ancient scrolls.

events.title: Second Vatican Council
events.note: The twenty-first ecumenical council of the Roman Catholic Church, opened by John XXIII and closed by Paul VI, issued four constitutions, nine decrees and three declarations. Protestant and Orthodox observers were invited to attend.

source.work: Xavier University, Jesuit Resource
source.locator: Resources by Theme: Vatican Council II
source.quote: It opened on October 11, 1962 under the pontificate of Pope John XXIII and closed on December 8, 1965 under Pope Paul VI.

second_source.work: The Holy See, Paul VI
second_source.locator: Apostolic Brief "In Spiritu Sancto" for the Closing of the Council, December 8, 1965
second_source.quote: Therefore we decided to close for all intents and purposes, with our apostolic authority, this same ecumenical council called by our predecessor, Pope John XXIII, which opened October 11, 1962, and which was continued by us after his death.

events.title: Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy
events.note: A summit of the International Council on Biblical Inerrancy adopted nineteen articles of affirmation and denial on the inerrancy of Scripture. Signers included J. I. Packer, R. C. Sproul, Francis Schaeffer and Carl F. H. Henry.

source.work: Dallas Theological Seminary, Turpin Library Archives
source.locator: International Council on Biblical Inerrancy (ICBI) collection
source.quote: Summit I met in Chicago on October 26–28, 1978. Over 300 Christian leaders, theologians and pastors attended and adopted the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy, consisting of nineteen articles with brief exposition.

second_source.work: Southwestern Baptist Theological Seminary
second_source.locator: Affirmed Statements: Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy, Background
second_source.quote: The “Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy” was produced at an international Summit Conference of evangelical leaders, held at the Hyatt Regency O’Hare in Chicago in the fall of 1978.
